text:
TSMC's Three CPO Paths: The Physics of Bandwidth Multiplication and the Engineering of Yield Division

TSMC($TSM )'s accelerated push into co-packaged optics can be quantified along three parallel expansion paths: raising per-lane speed from 200 Gbps toward 400 Gbps and beyond, widening optical channel count from 16 to 32, 64, and beyond, and introducing wavelength-division multiplexing so a single fiber carries multiple wavelengths simultaneously. If all three advance in tandem, the bandwidth curve doubles roughly every two years — from a 3.2 Tbps baseline today toward a theoretical 128x by 2040, implying a path into the hundreds of terabits.

Those numbers deserve scrutiny, but the more useful question is why the CPO bandwidth curve can exhibit this kind of regularity — and what constrains it from translating into production output on the roadmap's cadence.

The physics behind the bandwidth wall
The starting point is a structural mismatch that is now being quantified. An SK Hynix research roadmap published in Nature Electronics puts hardware compute throughput growth at roughly 3x every two years, while interconnect bandwidth grows at only about 1.4x over the same period. The gap between these two rates widens continuously, forming what SK Hynix calls the bandwidth wall.

The physical basis is the energy ceiling of copper interconnect. Conventional copper cabling consumes over 10 pJ/bit. As AI cluster scale expands from thousands of GPUs to tens of thousands and transmission distance extends from in-rack to rack-to-rack, copper's power consumption and signal attenuation worsen in tandem. Beyond 200G, signal attenuation becomes severe after traversing longer copper paths through ABF substrates, PCBs, and connectors, pushing the industry toward shortened copper paths and elongated optical paths — moving the electro-optical conversion element ever closer to the ASIC to reduce power, latency, and signal loss.

Silicon photonics currently achieves 2.4 to 5 pJ/bit, versus 12 to 15 pJ/bit for 2024-era copper systems — a reduction of more than two-thirds. In thousand-GPU AI clusters, this efficiency differential translates into megawatt-level power differences, which is the direct driver behind CPO's transition from optional to necessary.

Three paths, one multiplicative effect
TSMC's three paths are not independent technology choices. They correspond to three distinct physical dimensions of optical interconnect, each with its own engineering constraints.

The first path — per-lane speed from 200G toward 400G — depends on modulator performance. TSMC Vice President Hsu Kuo-chin said on August 31 that COUPE will mass-produce the world's first single-channel 200 Gbps micro-ring modulator in 2026, with 400 Gbps modulators doubling that rate subsequently. The micro-ring modulator is critical because its footprint is far smaller than a conventional Mach-Zehnder modulator, making it suitable for high-density integration within a compact package; it has demonstrated a bit error rate below one in a billion.

The second path — channel count from 16 to 32, 64, and beyond — involves the density of the fiber array unit. FAU has been formally incorporated into the COUPE bandwidth expansion roadmap, shifting from a peripheral component to a core interface of the optical engine. Multi-row FAU adoption means the number of fibers integrated in a single fiber bundle multiplies, with corresponding increases in precision alignment requirements.

The third path — wavelength-division multiplexing — is the most systemically complex. It requires integrating multiple laser sources and modulators of different wavelengths within the same optical engine and ensuring wavelength selectivity at the demultiplexing end meets bit error rate requirements. TSMC's two strategies — "Fast and Narrow" raising per-lane speed, and "Slow and Wide" increasing channel density through WDM and multi-row FAU — are not mutually exclusive at the system level but combined according to application scenario.

The combined effect of all three advancing simultaneously — per-lane speed doubling times channel count doubling times wavelength count doubling — forms the mathematical basis for bandwidth doubling every two years. By 2030, TSMC plans to raise bandwidth density from 0.5 Tbps per millimeter to 4 Tbps, an eightfold increase in four years.

The yield multiplication: an engineering problem, not a manufacturing one
The technical feasibility of the bandwidth path is established. But the industrialization bottleneck sits at a more fundamental level.

CPO system yield is a multiplication problem, not an addition problem. Assume a CPO system integrates 32 optical engines — considering that each optical engine in Nvidia's Spectrum-X CPO switch contains 16 200G optical channels, high-end configurations require multiple engines in parallel. At an individual engine yield of 95%, the system integration yield equals 0.95 to the 32nd power, approximately 19%.

SemiAnalysis adopted this calculation logic in its June 2026 report "Powered Down, Lights Off," arriving at a system-level yield of about 19.4%, far below the threshold for scalable profitability. That calculation triggered a reassessment of CPO production timelines, with SemiAnalysis concluding that large-scale CPO production would be delayed to 2028 or 2029 — significantly behind prior market expectations. AAOI fell 17.17% that day, and Coherent dropped 11.44%.

An important qualification: the calculation assumes yield failures occur independently at each serial stage, meaning defective units from earlier stages are not screened out before entering the next stage. If front-end testing can effectively filter non-conforming units before optical engines enter system assembly, the yield base for subsequent assembly is 100% rather than 95%, and the system yield calculation changes materially. This dispute's substance is that CPO's core production bottleneck is not manufacturing itself but whether testing can perform defect screening at the right position, at acceptable cost and time.

Morgan Stanley's supply chain research identifies the improvement vector. Insertion 2 wafer-level testing — the first node that validates both electrical and optical signals simultaneously — has compressed from one wafer per day in the second half of 2025 to approximately six hours per wafer currently, with a target of three to four hours per wafer within the next six to twelve months. Testing efficiency directly determines front-end screening throughput, and front-end screening throughput determines whether the yield multiplication formula holds. Without testing efficiency gains, sufficient PIC capacity cannot translate into actual shipments.

TSMC is advancing wafer-level edge coupler testing, aiming to complete CP testing at the wafer stage and screen defective components before they enter expensive advanced packaging processes. The logic: perform as much defect screening as possible at the lowest-cost stage of packaging, avoiding resource waste when defective units enter subsequent high-cost steps.

Competitive landscape: differentiated positioning across three routes
TSMC's COUPE platform is not the only CPO path. Broadcom, Nvidia, Samsung, and Intel have each selected different technology routes and customer positioning.

Broadcom is the CPO production pioneer. Its 51.2T Bailly CPO switch has entered small-volume production, with Delta Electronics and Micas Networks assisting volume introduction, achieving up to 70% power reduction versus conventional pluggable optical transceivers, and having completed deployment validation with Meta and other hyperscalers.

Nvidia's CPO strategy reflects stronger vertical integration. The Spectrum-X CPO switch, using TSMC's COUPE packaging, entered full production in August 2026, covering Spectrum 6810 (102.4T) and Spectrum 6800 (409.6T), integrating second-generation 3.2T optical engines with 16 200G optical channels each. The switch achieves laser count reduction of 4x, power reduction of 5x, and MTBI improvement of 10x. Nvidia's distinctive approach is a unified photonics strategy — using the same optical hardware across Quantum, Spectrum, and NVLink switches to minimize manufacturing cost. In the Vera Rubin platform, Nvidia introduced CPO-based NVLink switches to create NVL576 (8-rack) pods, extending CPO from the network layer to the compute interconnect layer.

Samsung chose a foundry positioning rather than chip design. Its roadmap shows 2027 for thermocompression-bonded optical engines, 2028 for transition to hybrid bonding, and 2029 for turnkey CPO foundry service — customers provide designs, Samsung delivers chips, packaging, coupling, and testing. Samsung has secured optical communication orders and plans to begin large-scale production in the second half of 2026, while negotiating commercial cooperation with several major global customers.

Intel focuses on extending its EMIB-T packaging route into optical interconnect, leveraging its differentiated advanced packaging capability. At the foundry level, GlobalFoundries acquired Advanced Micro Foundry in November 2025, establishing what it claims is the largest pure-play silicon photonics foundry, expanding capacity and R&D in Singapore.

The structural implication of this competitive landscape is that the CPO value chain's profit pool distribution differs from the pluggable optical module era. In the pluggable era, value accrued primarily at the optical module packaging stage. In the CPO era, value shifts toward chip design (Broadcom, Nvidia), advanced packaging (TSMC), and system integration — compressing the bargaining power of traditional optical module packagers.

Capacity path and financial transmission
TSMC's capacity buildout provides a quantified industrialization path. Its PIC capacity expansion starts from roughly 500 wafers per month currently, reaching 10,000 per month in Q2 2026, 15,000 in Q4 2026, and exceeding 25,000 by 2028 — a more than 30x expansion in three years. Each wafer accommodates 648 dies, implying annual PIC output of up to 194 million units.

The loss from capacity to actual shipments is significant. At a 50% SoIC integration yield, 10,000 wafers per month can produce roughly 2 million optical engines, but downstream packaging losses may reduce actual shipments to approximately 390,000 units. Morgan Stanley projects global CPO switch shipments reaching approximately 23,000 units in 2026 — led by Nvidia's 100T switches — rising to 59,000 in 2027 and 200,000 by 2030. If yield continues improving, actual optical engine shipments corresponding to TSMC's 2027 PIC capacity could reach approximately 7.8 million units.

On customer adoption cadence, 2026–2027 is led by Nvidia, Broadcom, and AMD adopting TSMC's COUPE platform, followed by MediaTek, Marvell, and Ayar Labs expected to join the volume platform in 2028. This diffusion path means CPO will penetrate from flagship switch products into the broader ASIC and networking chip market.

TSMC's gross margin in the second half of 2026 may face erosion from initial 2nm production and overseas fab costs, but its leading-edge pricing power provides a hedge — 2nm wafer pricing is expected to approach $30,000, and price increases can effectively offset cost pressure. CPO as an incremental advanced packaging segment carries pricing logic similar to CoWoS: packaging value rises with chip complexity, and TSMC's pricing power in high-end packaging is not constrained by foundry capacity competition.

What to track
Three signals will determine whether the CPO bandwidth path translates from roadmap into verifiable industrial cadence.

Whether Insertion 2 test time compresses to three to four hours per wafer by 2027. Morgan Stanley identifies this metric as the core bottleneck converting CPO capacity into shipments. Test time directly determines front-end screening throughput, and screening efficiency determines whether the yield multiplication formula holds. Without compression, even ample PIC capacity cannot yield sufficient optical engine shipments.

The CPO adoption node in Nvidia's Feynman architecture. Nvidia's CPO roadmap extends from switch CPO in Blackwell, to NVLink CPO in Vera Rubin, to potential PIC-ASIC 3D vertical integration in Feynman. Supply chain surveys indicate CoPoS technology has been incorporated into Nvidia's Feynman GPU architecture blueprint, with the 2029 Feynman Ultra version expected to fully adopt the architecture. If Feynman's CPO adoption proceeds on schedule, CPO extends from the switching layer to the compute layer, materially expanding the addressable market.

Samsung's CPO foundry customer adoption cadence. Samsung plans to offer turnkey CPO foundry service in 2029, having already secured optical communication orders with large-scale production planned for the second half of 2026. If Samsung successfully onboards major customers between 2028 and 2029, it would pose a substantive challenge to TSMC's dominance in CPO foundry; if customer adoption lags, TSMC's COUPE platform will retain its first-mover advantage.

The CPO bandwidth path's regularity — doubling every two years — is physically feasible. Whether that regularity translates into industrial cadence depends on the coordinated evolution of three variables: test efficiency, yield engineering, and customer adoption. Bandwidth density improvement is a determined technical direction; manufacturability improvement is an uncertain engineering challenge. The time gap between the two is the key variable determining CPO's industrialization pace. TSMC has defined the slope of the bandwidth curve through three parallel paths, but whether that curve delivers on the roadmap's cadence depends on whether yield engineering — this division problem — can approach unity at every serial node.

Understand that Texas could fill *all* of its UT campuses with kids scoring 1200 or higher on the SAT. All of them. So the notion that oh, it's ok that the lower schools admit incompetents is just bullshit.  But that's the story.

So no, a good kid can't now go to UTEP as a freshman. It's a billion times better to go to a community college for two years and transfer to a better campus when the diversity yutzes aren't counting.

text:
At 24, She Took Her Seat in the Cockpit of China’s Largest Transport Aircraft
24岁，她坐进了中国最大运输机的驾驶舱

Li Xueran, a post‑2000s female pilot, now serves as co‑pilot of the Y‑20, China’s large‑scale strategic transport aircraft.

Recruited into the military at 19, she reached the Y‑20 cockpit by age 24. Over five years, she transformed from an ordinary high‑school student into a large transport‑aircraft pilot. Her story is no legend of innate genius. Instead, it offers a genuine account of a Chinese Gen‑Z young person refining herself relentlessly under high‑pressure conditions to build professional competence step‑by‑step.

## A Spontaneous Application “Just for a Friend” Changed Her Life

Li Xueran had dreamed of joining the military since childhood, yet she never imagined she could become a pilot — it felt far beyond her reach.

In her senior year of high school, an Air Force pilot‑recruitment presentation came to her school. Teachers asked her and another female classmate to sit in on the session. Inspired by the briefing, her classmate resolved to apply. Li Xueran signed up merely to accompany her friend, viewing it as nothing more than a routine medical check‑up. Unexpectedly, she passed more than 100 screening tests one after another. By the secondary assessment stage, the thick stack of application forms had dwindled to a slim handful. At that moment, a thought crossed her mind: maybe I really can do this. In the end, she became the only female flight cadet admitted that year across the three northeastern provinces of China.

This detail merits attention: her admission was no token gesture, but the hard‑won outcome of fierce competition.

## First Lesson in Barracks: Romantic Fantasies Give Way to Extreme Training

Upon entering military camp, her romantic visions of flying quickly collided with harsh reality.

Physical conditioning, aviation theories and flight techniques daily pushed her physical and mental endurance to the limit. Training was designed not only to test one’s stamina, but also the ability to maintain precision under immense pressure.

Li Xueran later recalled that the most vital lesson she learned in those years was to manage fear, fatigue and self‑doubt. In aviation, even a tiny mistake could escalate into serious trouble. Cadets therefore had to drill complex procedures until they became instinctive reflexes.

## The Toughest Hurdle: Staying Calm When the Aircraft “Misbehaves”

Aerobatic flight training marked her most stressful period.

During aerial manoeuvres, instrument gauges fluctuated wildly while her body endured extreme g‑forces. Human instinct urges panic in such moments. Rather than relying on raw courage to push through, Li Xueran repeatedly rehearsed every sequence of movements, throttle adjustments and gaze shifts on the ground, until the whole routine turned into muscle memory.

On assessment day, she remained surprisingly composed while executing the manoeuvres. After landing, her palms were soaked in sweat, yet she felt an unprecedented sense of reassurance.

This was not confidence born of “never being afraid”, but confidence stemming from “being fully prepared”.

## A “Naturally‑Gifted Pilot”? She Questions the Label

Some people call Li Xueran a naturally‑gifted pilot, a label she does not fully embrace.

In her eyes, gifted peers abound around her. What truly matters is how one makes use of whatever talent they possess. Between 19 and 24, she dedicated herself almost entirely to one goal: earning her place beneath the blue sky.

This mindset is far from unique among Chinese Gen‑Z. A growing number of young people are stepping into high‑threshold fields including engineering, medicine, aviation and technology. They believe competence is not innate, but forged through consistent devotion.

## From Basic Trainer to Y‑20: Every Stage Means Starting Anew

Li Xueran graduated top of her class from basic trainer aircraft training. The outstanding result qualified her for further training, yet it brought no easy path ahead. She then transitioned to the Y‑7 transport aircraft, and after rounds of rigorous evaluations, qualified as co‑pilot for the Y‑20.

The Y‑20, codenamed “Kunpeng”, is China’s domestically‑developed large long‑range military transport aircraft. For young pilots, stepping into its cockpit means largely starting over: its systems are far more sophisticated, responsibilities heavier, and margins for error narrower.

Li Xueran shared that when she first entered the Y‑20 cockpit, the sea of dials and control sticks drove home a stark truth: all she had learned before laid only the foundation, and the real challenges were just beginning.

## A Contingent of Female Transport Pilots Averaging 22 Years Old

The unit of female transport pilots Li Xueran belongs to has an average age of merely 22.

This statistic illustrates that young Chinese pilots are entrusted with genuine operational responsibilities at an early stage. Far from remaining in the background as mere observers, they train for real‑world missions: operating complex systems, managing flight workflows, and undertaking transport and support assignments.

China has steadily expanded female participation in military aviation in recent years. Li Xueran’s story reflects a clear trend: young women are no longer rare exceptions in technical military roles, but are becoming the new normal of the younger generation.

This year marks the 10th anniversary of the official commissioning of the Y‑20 in Chinese military service. For Li Xueran, the milestone is more than a number. Her story could easily be simplified into a feel‑good inspirational tale, yet it deserves deeper reflection.

She embodies a cohort of young Chinese people: stepping early into highly demanding technical professions, embracing pressure as part of growth, and measuring themselves against professional standards rather than outside praise.

From that high‑school pilot‑recruitment briefing to her seat inside the strategic transport aircraft cockpit, Li Xueran’s journey is more than a personal achievement. It serves as a window showing how China’s younger generation is trained, tested, and empowered to take on roles once deemed out of reach.

    李雪冉，一位"00后"女飞行员，如今已是中国大型战略运输机运-20的副驾驶。
    从19岁招飞入伍到24岁飞上运-20，她用五年时间完成了从普通高中生到大型运输机飞行员的蜕变。她的故事不是"天赋异禀"的传奇，而是一个中国Z世代年轻人在高压环境中反复打磨自己、一步步走向专业的真实记录。

【一次"陪朋友试试"的报名，改变了人生方向】
    李雪冉从小想当兵，但从没想过自己能成为飞行员——那太遥远了。
    高三那年，空军招飞宣讲来到她的学校。老师安排她和另一位女同学去旁听。同学听完后热血沸腾，决心报考；李雪冉则是抱着"陪她试试，反正就当体检"的心态报了名。没想到，初选100多项检查，她一关一关闯了过来。到了复选阶段，报名表从厚厚一摞缩减为薄薄一小沓。那一刻，她心里冒出一个念头：也许我真的可以。最终，她成为那一年中国东北三省唯一被录取的女飞行学员。
    这个细节值得关注——她的入选不是象征性的，而是实打实竞争出来的结果。

【军营里的第一课：浪漫想象让位于极限训练】
    踏进军营后，关于飞行的浪漫想象很快被现实击碎。
    体能训练、航空理论、飞行技术，每一天都在挑战身体和意志的极限。训练的目的不仅是看谁能扛住，更是看谁能在高压下保持精准。
    李雪冉后来回忆说，那几年她学会的最重要的事，是如何控制恐惧、疲劳和自我怀疑。在航空领域，一个微小的失误可能演变为严重问题。因此，学员必须把复杂操作练成本能反应。

【最难的一关：当飞机"不听话"时保持冷静】
    学习特技飞行是她压力最大的阶段。
    空中翻转时，仪表盘数据剧烈跳动，身体承受异常过载，人的本能反应是慌张。李雪冉的应对方式不是靠勇气硬扛，而是在地面反复推演每一个动作衔接、油门配合、视线转移，直到整套流程变成肌肉记忆。
    考核那天，真正做起动作时她反而异常平静。落地后手心全是汗，但心里有一种从未有过的踏实感。
    那不是"从没害怕过"的自信，而是"已经准备好了"的自信。

【"天赋型选手"？她不完全认同这个标签】
    有人称李雪冉是"天赋型选手"。她自己并不完全接受。
    在她看来，身边最不缺的就是有天赋的人。真正重要的是你怎么对待天赋。从19岁到24岁，她几乎只做了一件事：让自己配得上头顶那片蓝天。
    这种心态在中国Z世代中并不罕见。越来越多年轻人进入工程、医学、航空、科技等高门槛领域，他们相信能力不是天生的，而是靠持续投入换来的。

【从初教机到运-20：每一步都是重新开始】
    初教机结业，李雪冉综合排名第一。这个成绩帮她拿到了继续前进的资格，但并没有让下一步变得轻松。她随后改装运-7，又通过层层考核，最终成为运-20的副驾驶。
    运-20是中国自主研发的大型远程军用运输机，代号"鲲鹏"。对于年轻飞行员来说，进入它的驾驶舱意味着在很多方面从头学起——系统更复杂，责任更重大，容错空间更小。
    李雪冉说，第一次走进运-20驾驶舱时，满眼的仪表和操纵杆让她立刻明白：之前学到的一切只是基础，真正的考验才刚刚开始。

【一群平均年龄22岁的女运输机飞行员】
    李雪冉所在的女运输机飞行员队伍，平均年龄只有22岁。
    这个细节说明，中国的年轻飞行员正在被快速赋予实际责任。她们不是待在后方"见习"，而是在为执行真实任务做准备——操作复杂系统、管理飞行流程、承担运输保障任务。
    中国近年来持续扩大女性在军事航空领域的参与。李雪冉的故事折射出一个趋势：年轻女性在技术型军事岗位中不再是罕见的例外，而是正在成为新一代的常态。
    今年是中国运-20正式列装十周年。对李雪冉来说，这个节点不只是数字。她的故事很容易被包装成一个简单的励志叙事。但它比那更值得关注。
    她代表着一批中国年轻人：很早就进入高要求的技术领域，把压力视为成长的一部分，用专业标准而非外界评价来衡量自己。
    从高中招飞宣讲到坐上战略运输机的驾驶舱，李雪冉的经历不只是个人成就，更是一扇窗口——让人看到中国年轻一代如何被训练、被考验、被推向曾经看似遥不可及的岗位。

text:
One of the hardest questions in state-building is not whether a state can survive a crisis, but whether it can convert crisis-generated capacity into durable political power.

Iraq’s experience from 2014 to 2018 offers an important test. The state faced an existential security threat, severe fiscal pressure, multiple centers of power, and a fragmented decision environment. Crisis temporarily strengthened executive authority, accelerated decision-making, expanded resource mobilization, and increased the importance of coalition management and diplomatic leverage.

But successful crisis leadership does not automatically create a more capable state.

The real test comes afterward: did emergency capacity become embedded in the state’s decision architecture, strengthen strategic autonomy, and expand the political center’s ability to convert resources, legitimacy, partnerships, and diplomatic access into sustained strategic effect?

Usable strategic power begins where resources, political authority, institutional coordination, and diplomatic leverage can be converted into sustained state action.

That is the distinction between temporary crisis capacity and usable strategic power.

The more demanding measure of leadership is whether power remains dependent on exceptional circumstances—or becomes an institutional capability the state can reproduce after the crisis has passed.

Tradition is treated as a “judge” of revelation. But treating tradition as a “judge” of revelation, however, reverses the relationship between revelation and tradition, subordinating the revelation of Allah to the “judgment” of men. 
Tradition was treated as a “root” of legislation. But legislation in Islam is the exclusive prerogative of Allah. To treat tradition as a root of legislation is to treat their transmitters as “lawgivers.” This is shirk. 
Treating tradition as revelation enabled tradition to “abrogate” and “replace” revelation pertaining to apostasy and adultery. Allah prescribed the death penalty for neither. 
But jurists prescribe capital punishment for both. Hawkish jurists transformed parts of penal legislation into a “license to kill.” In this they transgressed the hudud of Allah.
Recourse to problematic perceptions was assisted by the repression of reason.  For which person in his or her right mind would agree that tradition is revelation? 
The reluctance to use reason was justified by recourse to a tradition in which using reason to understand revelation is treated as kufr. This produced adverse effects.
The reluctance to engage reason prevents Muslims from understanding revelation. A few verses began to strike them as “unclear.” 
The required “clarification” would be provided by tradition. They presumed that persons “explain” better than Allah. 
The treatment of tradition as a “judge” of revelation was also justified by the perception that revelation is in parts “insufficiently detailed.” 
But revelation presents itself as “clear” and “fully detailed.” Why would a Book that is “clear” and “fully detailed” require further clarification and detailing? 
The perception that the Book is in parts “unclear” and “insufficiently detailed” requires rejecting all verses that teach the contrary. This is tantamount to kufr. 
The perceptions that the Book is in parts “unclear” and “insufficiently detailed” accordingly render all exegesis and jurisprudence built upon them unreliable.
Renewal requires the desacralization of tradition, the affirmation of the pre-eminence of revelation and the rehabilitation and re-engagement of reason. 
This requires a rehabilitation of the knowledge of revelation. It also requires the rehabilitation of the epistemology of revelation, both exegesis and jurisprudence. 
Exegesis and jurisprudence resting on flawed assumptions is not equipped to generate reliable results. 
The alleged “explanation” and “detailing” revelation by tradition, rather than “clarifying” and “detailing” revelation, corrupted the knowledge of revelation. 
In fact, it brought a new religion, a religion if war. This religion is based on tradition presented as “revelation” and the alleged “abrogation” of all verses of reconciliation by the verse of the sword. 
The teaching of war enabled the misrepresentation of Islam as a teaching of war. It enabled treating jihad al-talab as a sixth pillar of Islam. 
The perception that the umma is in a state of war between the dar al-Islam and the dar al-harb embroiled the umma in wars that brought defeat. 
"The immediate cause of the Mongol invasion can be attributed to a grievous mistake of ‘Alauddin Muhammad, the Shah of Khwarism. A body of traders who had arrived from Mongolia was put to death, and when Chengiz Khan deputed an embassy to enquire into the reasons for it, Muhammad replied by killing the envoy too. On receiving the news of this outrage upon international courtesy, the Mongol Khakan Chengiz Khan let loose the whirlwind of savagery upon the world of Islam." History repeated itself at Vienna.
"In 1529 the Ottoman Empire made a determined effort to capture Vienna, the capital of the Hapsburg Austrian Empire. The failure to take Vienna marked the end of Turkish expansion into Europe…In 1529, Suleiman launched a campaign against Austria’s Archduke Ferdinand I with an army of more than 100,000. 
Suleiman’s advance from the Black Sea, which began in May, was arduous because the weather had been particularly wet, with many lives lost due to the spread of illnesses through the soaked ranks of the sultan’s army. Much of the heavy artillery that would have been vital in the siege had to be abandoned when it became stuck in mud…Attack after attack was repulsed by the Austrian defenders, who picked off the Ottoman troops with arquebuses from the high walls of the city and forced back those who scaled the walls by using long pikes….Suleiman then ordered a retreat of his battered army, which turned into a disastrous ordeal as winter snows came early causing many deaths and loss of the remaining artillery."  
An additional example of jihad al-talab is the ill-fated Siege of Vienna, from July 17 to September 12, 1683.
"The leader of the Hungarian Calvinists, Imre Thokoly, appealed to the Ottoman grand vizier, Kara Mustafa, to attack the Habsburg capital…Ottoman forces had made serious inroads into the city’s defenses and are generally believed to have come closer to taking Vienna than they were in 1529. The battle raged for 15 hours before the Ottoman invaders were driven from their trenches. The red tent of the grand vizier was blown up, but he escaped while thousands of members of his routed army were slaughtered or taken prisoner.  
The end of the siege marked the beginning of the end of Ottoman domination in eastern Europe."  
Muslims were defeated in France, by the Mongols in 1258, and at the gates of Vienna in 1529 and 1683. 
The recording of traditions was spurred by the perception that the prophet abrogated the prohibition of recording his traditions. 
"[N]o one before the reign of Caliph Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz has ever been reported to have said that the Prophet abrogated the hadith in which he forbade others to record the Sunnah.  
One of the first systematic attempts to set the hadiths down in writing was made by Caliphs Abd al-‘Aziz ibn Marwan (d. 86 ah/705 ce) and ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz (d. 101 ah/720 ce) – his son – together with the jurists of their day.  
Abbasid Caliph Ja’far al-Mansur (d. 158 ah/775 ce) once said to Imam Malik [d. 795]: “Write a book whose contents I can require people to adhere to...”   
‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz [d. 720] and Abu Ja’far al-Mansur were thus in agreement concerning the importance of compiling knowledge that went back to the time of the Companions in Madinah. ‘Umar had instructed Abu Bakr ibn Hazm [d. 737] to undertake such a collection, while Abu Ja’far al-Mansur instructed Imam Malik to do the same.  
As Caliphs ‘Abd al-‘Aziz and his son ‘Umar viewed things, the purpose behind the collection of narratives about the Prophet’s life was not to create a corpus of additional or autonomous legislative evidence that would stand alongside the Qur’an, since the Qur’an’s relationship to the Sunnah was such that it would not have allowed for this kind of understanding. However even the best of medicines can have unwanted side effects, and the side effect that accompanied the collection of oral narratives was that – just as the leaders of the first Muslim generation had feared and cautioned against – people became so preoccupied with these narratives that they lost their focus on the Qur’an."  According to Daniel Brown:
"Another focus of debate is the historical tradition that states that the first individual to record the hadith, under orders from the Caliph Hisham [ibn Abd al-Malik, d. 743], was the traditionist Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri (d. 742). There is fairly wide agreement among Muslim scholars on the authenticity of this tradition, but disagreement over what it signifies. The tradition has commonly been taken to mean that al-Zuhri, under duress, became the first traditionist to violate the Prophet’s prohibition on recording hadith in writing. Al-Zuhri is reported to have said: “We disapproved of recording knowledge until these rulers forced us to do so. After that we saw no reason to forbid the Muslims to do so.” In other words, before al-Zuhri writing was the rare exception; after al-Zuhri writing of traditions became commonplace. This argument is bolstered by numerous accounts that early generations of pious Muslims, including not only al-Zuhri and traditionists like him but also the first four Caliphs, strongly disapproved of writing hadith." 
The turn to tradition traditions was assisted by the repression of reason. Reason was perceived as unfit to understand revelation. 
The repression of reason was due partly to political reasons. People who do not use their reason are easier to control. 
The repression of reason was bolstered by a flawed understanding of the relationship between reason and revelation. 
For under the influence of tradition, including sufism, reason was perceived as an enemy of revelation. 
But reason and revelation are not enemies; rather reason is required to understand revelation. But reason is required not just to understand but also to follow revelation. 
"Many orthodox Islamic scholars went to the extreme of denying reason and its role, thus limiting Islamic thought to literalist and descriptive studies of the revealed texts that have continued to influence Islamic thought by making it suspicious even today of all forms of rational inquiry. 
Revelation addresses all aspects of life. By contrast, tradition is truncated; essential parts of the teaching of revelation are absent. 
Revelation emphasises justice, ethics, and reason; but we find few books addressing justice, reason or ethics in the traditions. 
But there is a plethora of traditions explaining the way to pray. What explains this aberration? The treatment of tradition as “revelation from God” enabled the fusion of tradition and revelation. But the fusion brought confusion. 
Blurring the difference between tradition and revelation enabled traditions to “judge,” “abrogate” and even “replace” parts of revelation. Recourse to the teaching of abrogation corrupted the knowledge of revelation. 
When reasoning atrophies, knowledge deteriorates. In Islam, using reason to understand revelation was associated with kufr, based on a problematic tradition. As a result, reasoning deteriorated and produced a “crisis in the Muslim mind.” 
The disparagement of reasoning made it hard to comprehend and follow revelation. It tainted the knowledge of revelation and triggered the fall of the empire. 
Will any nation flourish without the use of reason? Reason is the key to knowledge. The acquisition of knowledge requires using reason. To reject reason is to throw away the key to knowledge, to fall into ignorance. 
The renewal of the Muslim civilization requires recovering the knowledge of revelation, which presupposes the rehabilitation and re-engagement of reason for the purpose of comprehending and following revelation. 
The Islamic civilization is not what it used to be. At the time of the golden age, it was at its pinnacle. This was due to revelation.
"No other sacred scripture has ever had a similarly immediate impact upon the lives of the people who first heard its message and, through them and the generations that followed them, on the entire course of civilisation.”  
However, the Muslim civilization waned. Muslims drifted from revelation and preferred to follow tradition: 
"the reality being lived at present by the Muslim nation appears to be at complete odds with the guidance embodied in the message and vision conveyed in the Holy Qur’an." 
What were the factors that triggered the disintegration of the Muslim civilization? Was there anything that altered the Islamic worldview?
"[W]e need to know why and how, with the passing of the centuries, this worldview lost its influence, effectiveness, and dynamism to the point where the Muslim community of today has become weak, passive, and even persecuted.”
The ummah used to adhere to revelation; “God has given us the Qur’anic worldview as a guide.”  This worldview was a reiteration of the revelations given to all prior messengers.
"This Qur’anic revelation is the Law which God commanded His messengers, and all Muslims, to adhere to. Any interpretation of this Law must have a Qur’anic basis and be consistent with Qur’anic evidence." 
But the community was not content with following revelation. It turned from revelation to the predecessors and followed their ways rather than revelation. 
"The process of cultural, intellectual, and doctrinal distortion eventually reached crisis proportions: things had now reached the point where – given the ubiquity of fatalism, superstition, charlatanry, attempts to lend legitimacy to the status quo through distorted, truncated, and forged texts…the Islamic worldview had all but been lost."
The worldview that replaced it was problematic and even unIslamic. It featured a range of distortions. 
"Unfortunately…the predominant worldview among Muslims, which purports falsely to be ‘Islamic,’ is theoretical, atomistic, passive, and selective – its purpose being to justify or conceal a quasi-sacerdotal distortion of knowledge and the facts and the inability to master a comprehensive, objective scientific approach to research and analysis." 
By turning to tradition, the ummah embarked upon following a second guide: tradition. In turning from revelation to tradition, the umma turned from transcendental to man-made authority. But tradition could not and did not guide as well as revelation:
"[D]uring the days of the Prophet and the rightly guided caliphs, hadiths – that is, reports concerning something the Messenger of God had said, done, or approved – were not recorded with the accuracy and precision with which the Qur’an was recorded. The reason for this is simply that the Qur’an, rather than the hadiths, is the source of the timeless, abiding Islamic worldview." 
The turn from revelation to tradition produced adverse effects. It impeded the progress of the ummah by depriving it of the guidance offered by revelation. Moreover, the traditional ulema were against any change.
"The conservative reaction favours the status quo of the Muslims and abhors change in whatever form and under whatever banner. The upholders of this view are those scholars who accept the works of some authors (generally belonging to the 8 - 9th century A.H.) as the final and unquestionable authority on Islam. Any deviation from their stated opinion is regarded as a deviation from Islam itself…The door of ijtihad, they contend, is firmly closed because on the one hand no one is any more qualified for it and on the other there is no need for it. The authoritative books in use contain all the satisfactory answers to all the valid questions."
The rigidity of the ulema proved to be an impediment to reform. This was reinforced by excessive reverence for tradition. Thus, it has become necessary:
"to promote critical ability in the service of the study of Islam and to free the discipline from the dominance of past scholars whose authority is elevated in our traditional institutions to the level of the prophet (p.b.u.h.) and sometimes even above it. The word of the Imam of the Madhab is occasionally followed in defiance of the world of Allah (s.w.t)" 
For the errors of the ummah had lasting effects which require attention and resolution.
"[T]he errors into which the Muslim community fell early in its history have had long-lasting effects, thereby impeding its progress and depriving humanity for long centuries of the guidance offered by Islam and the divine revelation."
The turn from revelation to tradition proved problematic. Tradition did not prevent the umma from falling into confusion. 
"However, the traditional approach, in the manner it was presented and applied, did not prevent the Ummah from falling into a state of decline and failure, from which it is still suffering. Likewise, western thought, as it was presented and applied, cannot protect the Ummah from its inherent adverse, harmful, and even disastrous effects…this is conducive to a wide-ranging question: Is the Ummah going through a serious intellectual crisis, and, if so, how can it find its way out?"
It appears that indeed there is a crisis. But this is a crisis of thought. Hence, it has to be addressed on the intellectual level:
"[T]he crisis faced by the Ummah at the present time is one of thought…the crisis of its debilitation, factiousness, backwardness, and lack of civilization…It is therefore all the more important that we understand the nature of the crisis…Only if that is accomplished will we be able to penetrate to the heart of the crisis. Indeed, until now, it has been our ignorance of the nature of this crisis that has hampered us from evaluating our performance as a civilization and maintaining a course of progress over the centuries." 
It is advisable not be deterred by fears. It is necessary to address the paralysis of thought and use the intellect wisely: 
"[O]ur trepidations…about what we hold sacred…paralyze our minds and souls, and prevent us from thinking seriously, from pondering these matters, and from wisely using our intellect in ways that lead to true accomplishment." 
It is necessary to realize that reason has a role in the renewal of the Muslim civilization. For example, it is reason that enables us to distinguish wahy from fabrications of wahy. 
"Reason is the instrument humans use to understand, distinguish and compare insights, and it is the means of carrying out responsibilities in the seen world…It is reason which distinguishes between true wahy and false, between misleading lies, fabrications, and myths. Likewise, it is reason which enables humans to choose and face the consequences of the choices they make. 
It is reason that enables us to conduct analysis and make judgments in the process of renewal. Reason is instrumental in understanding.
Based on logic and the fundamentals of reason and common sense, we make observations and comparisons that enable us to form judgments about the world.” 
The turn to tradition proved problematic, as following different traditions brought disunity. “From the time the Muslim community abandoned the Qur’an and was overcome by confusion and error, its unity was lost.”  The energy of the ummah declined.
"Gradually Islam was no longer able to maintain its vitality. As a result, only the remnants of its spiritual teachings have survived over the centuries. The rest of its glorious civilization has perished."
The ummah today is a shadow of its former self: 
"the Ummah today and its youth might best be described as infirm, dissipated, unambitious, and lacking confidence."  
The trauma of the ummah is perceptible to any disinterested spectator. There is no point in pretending that it is business as usual.
"No one studying the Ummah will have difficulty in discerning the present backwardness of its culture, its political degradation, and its human suffering, regardless of its human and material resources and in spite of its values and principles. Such is the very heart of the Ummah's crisis. It is inevitable that such a backward and aimless existence should be of major concern…It is therefore only natural that the Ummah seeks to reform, renew, and revive itself."
There is a requirement to set priorities. 
"Reform must begin by rescuing the Muslim community from the distortions and falsehoods to which it has fallen prey."
The chief problem lies in thought: 
"It is obvious that the thought of the Ummah as it stands at present is in need of reform."
This is the responsibility of the ulema. 
"It is the responsibility of the Ummah's thinkers and scholars to return to Islamic thought its originality, integrity, and comprehensiveness. Only in this way can the deviations of the past be avoided."  
It is Muslim thought that requires reform: “when we speak of reform, we are really speaking of thought and the Muslim mind.”  Specifically, what is required is a reform of the methodology of thought. 
"It is clear that…what it is lacking is a methodology for sound thinking. Indeed, the problems of the Ummah are clearly connected to confused thinking, obscured social vision, improper and inadequate education, and the decline of its institutions in general. The result is that it is divided and has begun to resemble an enfeebled and cringing slave." 
The focus must be on the reform of Muslim thought, not on the reform of Islam. For the problems facing the Muslim ummah stem from a flawed methodology of thought. Thinking must be guided by an appropriate vision.
"The thinkers and scholars of the Ummah must focus their determination and attention first of all on the reform of Muslim thought and the clarification of its vision for the Ummah and its leadership."
In different words, the methodology of thought requires being reimagined and reconceptualized. 
"Islamic thought must undertake a methodological study to articulate…Islamic studies in various fields of life: politics, economics, psychology, education, the arts, and technology. Then, in the light of these general introductions, specialized methodologies may be established for each one of these fields. In this way, Islamic thought will be able to play its role in contributing to the social sciences. Islamic religious and educational institutions can no longer confine their studies to the texts of revelation, or remain isolated from the fields of social and technological studies."" 
The understanding of knowledge must be broadened to include present-day disciplines. For education is made up of more than religious education alone. 
We also require skills to gain employment in a contemporary economy. The process of renewal begins with a reform of thought. What is required is fresh thinking, past the cliches of the past. 
"In order for an Islamic movement to succeed in the modern Islamic world, it must first seek to reform the methodology of Islamic thought and the way it looks at civilization in general. Only in this way will the efforts and jihad of the Ummah rise above the oft-heard emotional and sentimental appeals that do nothing to produce the changes in thought and culture needed to combat contemporary challenges, to clarify the Ummah's identity and personality, or to recast its approaches and social institutions in an Islamic mold."  
Without a change in the methodology of thought, no meaningful change may be expected. The ummah will merely fall further behind the rest of the world. 
"Unless changes are made in methodology, no constructive efforts can take place, and no undertaking will amount to anything. In fact, such efforts represent a steady drain of valuable resources, while the gulf between the Ummah and the rest of the world grows even wider.

🔥 WHO DECIDES WHAT YOU EAT —
Food Culture & Culinary History 🍽️
🏭 THE MACHINE PLATE ▸ ▸ ▸ 📖 Post 22 OF 26
Roughly half the people alive are eating nitrogen pulled out of the air by a patent filed in 1908. The same chemistry is tied to somewhere between 100 and 150 million deaths in twentieth-century conflict.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

It begins with air.

Seventy-eight percent of the atmosphere is nitrogen, and almost none of it is usable. The molecule is locked — two atoms triple-bonded, inert, drifting through every lung on earth without being available to any of them. Plants need nitrogen to build protein and cannot take it from the air.

For the entire span of the previous seventeen posts, the only ways to get usable nitrogen into soil were manure, legumes, crop rotation, and mined deposits. Every one of those is a fixed and limited supply.

✅ On 13 October 1908, Fritz Haber filed a patent for a process that breaks the bond.

💡 Nitrogen out of the air, at industrial scale. It is the most consequential chemical reaction in the history of food, and there is nothing edible anywhere in it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📊 THE NUMBER

The figure that matters is not production tonnage. It is people.

📊 By 2008, Haber-Bosch nitrogen was supporting an estimated 48% of the global population — up from 44% in 2000.

📊 The same analysis estimates it has supported roughly 42% of global births over the past century.

📊 Global agricultural productivity, measured as persons fed per hectare, rose from 1.9 to 4.3 between 1908 and 2008.

📊 An independent assessment concluded global crop harvests would be roughly half their current level without nitrogen fertilizer.

✅ Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 1918.

🔒 Roughly one person in two now alive exists because of a patent filed in 1908. That is not a figure of speech. It is the estimate.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚠️ THE OTHER LEDGER

The same paper that produces the 48% figure carries a second number.

📊 Reactive nitrogen — the same chemistry, applied to munitions rather than fields — is linked to somewhere between 100 and 150 million deaths in twentieth-century conflict.

Nitrogen compounds are what explosives are made of. Before 1908, the supply of nitrates for munitions was as constrained as the supply for fertilizer, and for the same reason. The process that removed the ceiling on food production removed it on ammunition at the same moment, by the same chemistry, in the same country, on the eve of the same war.

⚠️ Haber's own wartime work extended beyond fertilizer. He is closely associated with the development of chemical weapons for use in the First World War.

🔒 The man who made it possible to feed half the planet also helped make it possible to gas an army. Both entries are in the same ledger, under the same name, arising from the same insight about a triple bond.

This series has spent seventeen posts declining to resolve things that cannot be resolved. This is the largest of them. There is no arithmetic that nets these figures against each other, and anyone who offers one is selling a conclusion.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌾 WHAT IT ACTUALLY CHANGED IN THE FIELD

Synthetic nitrogen did not simply raise yields. It changed what a farm is.

Under the old constraint, nitrogen came from within the system — manure from animals kept on the farm, legumes grown in rotation, fallow periods that rebuilt fertility. That constraint enforced diversity. A farm needed animals because it needed manure. It needed rotation because it needed nitrogen. Mixed farming was not an aesthetic preference; it was the only arrangement that worked.

📊 Remove the constraint and the rotation becomes optional. A field can grow the same high-yielding crop every year, with fertility delivered by truck.

⚠️ This is the mechanism behind the narrowing that runs through this entire series. Post 4's eleven independent centers of domestication produced an extraordinary diversity of crops. Post 13 showed what a narrow genetic base does when a pathogen finds it.

📊 Today, wheat, rice, and maize supply more than half the energy humanity obtains from plants — out of tens of thousands of edible species.

⚠️ That figure circulates in two forms and they are not the same claim. "More than half of plant-derived energy" is the conservative version. The higher figure often quoted — around 60% of total food energy intake — comes from a different calculation, and the two get used interchangeably by people who have not checked which one they are holding. This series uses the conservative form throughout, because the argument does not need the larger number and the larger number is harder to defend.

🔒 Post 1 opened by calling us the animal that will eat anything. The actual answer, in 2026, is three grasses.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔍 THE STEEL-MAN, AND THE CAVEAT

The strongest case for the industrial food system is the 48% figure, and it should be stated at full strength rather than acknowledged and hurried past.

Every romantic account of pre-industrial eating is written by someone who has never had to obtain a pre-industrial diet. Turn the clock back and most people would be working in a field or a kitchen all day, and many would be starving. The historical record does not contain a golden age of eating; it contains famine, seasonal hunger, monotony, and an enormous amount of unpaid labor, most of it female. Anybody proposing to undo the industrial food system is proposing, whether they have worked it out or not, to decide which half of the world's population is surplus.

⚠️ One caveat on the number itself, and it is a real one. A single global percentage conceals enormous variation. The share of people dependent on synthetic nitrogen is likely lower than 48% in high-income countries and higher in low-income ones.

⚖️ Which means the people most dependent on the industrial system are the ones with the least influence over how it runs — and the people with the most influence over the debate are the ones who could most easily eat without it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚠️ One more consequence belongs here. Nitrogen that does not stay in the field ends up in water, producing algal blooms and oxygen-depleted zones in rivers, lakes, and coastal waters. The fertilizer that feeds half the world degrades a portion of the fishery that feeds another part of it.

📊 And the alternative most often proposed is not new. Insects convert feed to protein far more efficiently than cattle, require less land and less water, and are already eaten regularly by at least two billion people. The technical case has been made for years. The obstacle is entirely cultural — and this series has spent seventeen posts showing where cultural obstacles come from.

Every earlier chapter had a person in it. A cook at a hearth, a scribe with a tablet, a cleric with a grudge, a critic with twelve friends.

This chapter has a chemist, a patent, and a number that describes half of everyone alive. Nobody eating today chose it, and almost nobody eating today knows it happened. The single most consequential decision about the human diet was made in a laboratory by a man who was not thinking about dinner.

🌿 Next: the movement that tried to take the decision back. Congress defined "organic" in 1990 and expected a working program by 1993; the seal arrived in 2002. What certification actually guarantees, what the yield and nutrition evidence genuinely shows in both directions, and what it would take to put that food in front of 29.4 million American schoolchildren.

📖 Post 22 of 26

Napoleon offered 12,000 francs in 1795 for a way to keep food from spoiling. The man who won it could not explain why his method worked, and neither could anyone else for fifty years.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

A peach in February used to be impossible. Not expensive — impossible, for everyone, everywhere north of where peaches grow.

That is the quiet limit running under every chapter before this one. Post 6's three-field rotation is a calendar. Post 8's salt monopoly exists because meat rots. Post 13's famine happens in a specific autumn. Food has always been a function of when and where it was grown, and every preservation technique in human history — drying, smoking, salting, fermenting — was a way of buying time against that limit.

📊 Then two technologies broke it, and the interval between them is under seventy years.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🥫 THE PRIZE

✅ In 1795 the French government offered 12,000 francs for a method of preserving food, driven by a straightforward military problem: larger armies needed regular supplies of edible food, and salted meat and hardtack were destroying the men eating them.

📊 Nicolas Appert, a confectioner, spent roughly fourteen years on it. His method was food in glass bottles, stoppered with cork, immersed in hot water. The full sterilization took about five hours.

📊 Samples went to sea with Napoleon's troops for over four months — partridge, vegetables, and gravy among eighteen items. They kept.

✅ He was awarded the prize in 1810, on condition that he publish. The resulting book described the process for more than fifty foods.

🔒 Appert had no idea why it worked. Louis Pasteur would not establish the role of microorganisms in spoilage for another half century. Appert's own reasoning was that if the method worked for wine, it should work for food.

💡 That is Post 6's finding arriving again in a new century. Fermentation ran for ten thousand years before anyone could explain it. Canning ran for fifty. People find the technique first and the reason second, if at all — and the technique works exactly as well either way.

⚠️ A detail worth noting about how invention actually travels. Later that same year, an English merchant named Peter Durand obtained a British patent for preserving food in tin and other metal vessels, having obtained a copy of Appert's book. Durand sold the patent on for £1,000. The tin can — lighter than glass, unbreakable in transport, better at conducting heat — is the version that went to the world.

⚠️ Appert died in poverty in 1841.

🔒 Post 15 has a man who invented the restaurant and died broke in 1806. This is the same story with a different object, thirty-five years later. The food system has a consistent record of not paying the people who build it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🪖 WHO IT WAS ACTUALLY FOR

Canning was not developed for households. It was a military logistics technology, and it stayed one for decades.

📊 Donkin's firm bought Durand's patent and began producing canned meat. The British navy was the main customer. The early "preserved provisions" were issued as medical stores for sick sailors.

📊 The term "bully beef" is generally traced to one of those early products — *bouilli*, boiled beef, in a tin.

📊 Canning reached American households through the same route: military demand in the Civil War, then commercial production. Salmon canneries in Maine and New Brunswick by the 1840s, condensed milk in the 1850s, automatic can-making machinery by the 1880s.

⚠️ And the can opener arrived decades after the can. The first tins were opened with a chisel and a hammer, because they had been designed for a navy that had both.

🔒 Post 17 showed a food-safety system arriving out of a spacecraft program. Canning arrived out of an army. Neither was invented to feed a family, and both ended up in every kitchen in the industrial world.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧊 THE SECOND BREAK

Canning defeats time. Refrigeration defeats distance, and it does something canning cannot: it keeps the food recognizable.

A canned peach is a different object from a peach. A chilled one is a peach. That distinction is the entire commercial value of the cold chain, and it is why refrigeration reorganized agriculture in a way canning never did.

The mechanism is a chain, not a machine — and every link has to hold. Cooling at the farm, a refrigerated railcar, a cold warehouse, a refrigerated ship, a chilled retail case, and eventually a box in the customer's kitchen. Break any link and the whole sequence is worthless.

⚠️ Building that chain took decades and enormous capital, and the result is the single largest change in what an ordinary person can eat.

🔒 Consider what it actually did. It decoupled where food is grown from where it is eaten. Cattle raised thousands of miles from the people who ate them. Fruit grown in one hemisphere for a winter in the other. Milk from a farm nobody in the city could name.

💡 Post 11 described sugar and tea arriving from colonies. Refrigeration extended that logic to everything perishable — which means the distance between the eater and the labor, engineered deliberately in the Atlantic sugar economy, became the default condition for the entire food supply rather than a feature of one trade.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🍽️ WHAT IT DID TO THE KITCHEN

For the professional reader, this is where the chapter lands.

Every technique in the classical repertoire that exists to manage spoilage — curing, confit, charcuterie, preserving, the entire architecture of the *garde manger* — was solving a problem that refrigeration solved better.

⚠️ They did not disappear. They changed category. A technique invented out of necessity became a technique practiced for flavor, which is a different craft with different standards and a different reason to exist.

📊 And the kitchen's daily rhythm changed with it. Escoffier's brigade in Post 17 is organized around stations. The cold chain is what makes it possible to stock those stations to a consistent standard, on a menu that does not change with the month, in a city with no agricultural hinterland.

🔒 The fixed menu is a refrigeration technology. So is the year-round ingredient list. So is the expectation that a restaurant in February can serve what it served in July.

⚖️ Whether that is gain or loss is genuinely arguable and this series will not settle it. What is not arguable is that it is a choice made possible by infrastructure, and that the seasonality a chef now chooses to cook by is a decision rather than a constraint.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚠️ THE COST NOBODY PUT ON THE INVOICE

Two costs belong on the record.

📊 The cold chain runs on energy, continuously, at every link, forever. Unlike canning — which spends energy once and then costs nothing to store — refrigeration is a permanent draw. A significant share of the food system's energy consumption is the simple act of keeping things cold.

⚠️ And the varieties changed to suit the chain. A fruit bred to survive refrigerated transit is bred for firmness, uniform ripening, and resistance to bruising. Those are shipping characteristics. They are not flavor characteristics, and where the two conflict, the shipping characteristic wins — because the fruit that arrives unsellable earns nothing regardless of how it tastes.

🔒 This is Post 4's narrowing, arriving in the produce aisle. The genetic base does not narrow because anyone decided flavor did not matter. It narrows because a supply chain applies a selection pressure, consistently, for a century — which is exactly the unconscious selection Darwin described and Post 4 traced in wheat.

💡 Nobody chose a tomato that tastes of nothing. A logistics system selected for one, the same way a sickle selected for a non-shattering spikelet.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Appert put food in a bottle because an army was dying of its own rations. What he actually did was sever the connection between when food is grown and when it is eaten — and refrigeration then severed the connection between where.

Everything in the two chapters that follow depends on both severances having already happened. A global fertilizer industry only makes sense if the grain can travel. A national organic standard only means something if the produce can reach a market. The infrastructure came first, quietly, built for soldiers and shareholders, and the arguments about what to put through it came after.

🧈 Next: a soap company took a fibre-mill waste product in 1911, hardened it into something resembling lard, and sold it as the modern, scientific choice. A century later the regulator declared it not safe.

NEWS: Sen. Bernie Moreno is publicly unloading on Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen over the stalled CLARITY Act, accusing him of criticizing the crypto bill without participating in months of negotiations.

Moreno says Van Hollen “hasn’t attended a single meeting” in 18 months to work through the legislation and argues the current bill contains unusually strict ethics provisions covering the president, vice president and other elected officials. The latest Senate text does include a new ethics section aimed at limiting how federal officeholders can profit from digital assets, although Democrats argue it still leaves major loopholes.

Van Hollen has been a consistent opponent of the bill in its current form. He introduced multiple amendments earlier this year dealing with elected officials’ crypto interests, consumer protections, and illicit finance, then voted against the legislation in committee when those concerns were not resolved to his satisfaction.

Moreno’s sharper point is procedural: Tuesday’s vote is to advance consideration of the bill, not necessarily to give final approval to every provision. He is effectively telling Van Hollen: get the bill onto the floor, offer amendments, and fight over the details there.

And the stakes are real. The Senate’s Sept. 15 procedural vote is shaping up as a major test for the legislation, which still needs bipartisan support to clear the chamber.

So this isn’t just another crypto argument anymore. It’s become a very Maryland-vs.-Ohio Senate fight over whether Congress regulates digital assets now — or leaves the current patchwork in place.

This is very long but worth the read, especially if you believe Trump hasn't accomplished anything. This should be read in every school room where our Government and History is supposed to be taught.

Trump’s Top 25 Achievements: 

The List Every Conservative Should Know and Use
Donald Trump doesn’t have an accomplishment problem. Republicans have an information problem. It’s on each of us to change that.

With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable when you consider that Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four.
Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so fast, across so many fronts that most people cannot keep up. The Enemedia buries the victories, while Republicans do an abysmal job of explaining them.
So here is the cheat sheet. It barely scratches the surface. And yet each and every item here is a game-changer.
This is not a list of promises. It’s a list of laws enacted, cases won, policies implemented, agreements secured, and measurable results.
You don’t have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump “hasn’t done much,” show them the receipts.
Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty

1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.

2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”
Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.

3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.
Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.

4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.
This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.
Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle

5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.
Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.

6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.
Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.

7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.
No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.

8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.

9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.

10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.
Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.

11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.
Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.
Trump Made Elections Matter Again

12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.
Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.
Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.

13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.
In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.

14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.
Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?

15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.
What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”

16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.
He Defended Faith and Family

17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.
Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.
He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.
No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.

18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.
Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.

19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.
That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.

20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.
He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First

21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.
Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.

22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.
Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.

23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.

24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.
Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.

25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.

After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.
Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.

Now Act Like It Matters

Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.
Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.
And let’s be clear. When you say (as some of you will) “the Republicans need to do a good enough job telling this story”, you’re pointing at yourself. You are “the Republicans.”

So tell people our story. Donald Trump is delivering great things, whether or not heaven on earth has broken out quite yet. Do the work, send the team he needs to Washington to finish the job, and get ready for 2028 afterward.

Take the time to learn at least five of these victories. Share this list with someone who needs it. And vote as though the most consequential Presidency in modern history depends on what you do.
