The human rights industry's favorite kind of victim is the politically useful one: the victim whose suffering can be attached to an adversary — a designated "villain" — preferably one that Western activists already know how to hate, pressure and organize against.

That is why Palestinian victims, when Israel can be cast as an alleged perpetrator of wrongs, generate an extraordinary machinery of outrage, while Sudanese victims of genocide, Afghan women under the Taliban, Iranian protesters murdered by their own regime, or persecuted Christians in Nigeria largely do not.

The hierarchy is not determined by the severity of the suffering; it is determined by the political usefulness of the victim and, even more importantly, by the identity of the "villain" supposedly committing these wrongs.

A United Nations fact-finding mission concluded in February 2026 that the mass executions, gang rapes and engineered starvation... in Sudan bore the hallmarks of genocide, and that genocidal intent was the only reasonable inference the evidence allowed.

The finding produced -- communiqués! No American campus has been covered with Sudanese encampments. No international campaign demands that corporations prove their innocence regarding Khartoum....

No permanent encampment stands outside Harvard demanding freedom for Afghan women, no divestment movement has become fashionable, no symbol has reached a red carpet. UN Women warns that the repression is being normalized.... The women remain where they were; the audience has left.
The West's response to Iran's January massacre took the form of diaspora rallies and a condemnation signed by 800 film professionals. The industry that produced five thousand signatures against Israeli film festivals produced eight hundred against a government that had just shot thousands of its own citizens in 48 hours, and its own trade press said so.

The American students who occupied buildings for Gaza risked nothing worse than a disciplinary hearing and offered the Iranian protesters nothing.

The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, which has spent seventeen years asking Washington to treat Nigeria as a country of particular concern, counts nearly 53,000 civilians killed there in targeted violence since 2009.

[A] successful cause needs more than victims. The favorite victim is not the one who suffers most, but the one whose suffering can be put to political use. A successful cause needs a usable "villain," ideally one already circulating in the narrative. Israel serves that purpose almost perfectly. It is Western-aligned, democratic, backed by Washington and permanently accessible to journalists. Its politicians answer questions, its courts rule against its government, and all of it can be pressured.

Western outrage has acquired a political economy: a successful cause needs more than victims. It needs a usable villain, ideally one already circulating in the narrative. Israel serves that purpose almost perfectly. It is Western-aligned, democratic, backed by Washington and permanently accessible to journalists. Its politicians answer questions, its courts rule against its government, and all of it can be pressured.

text:
CNN: Oman Was Set to Offer Voluntary Payments to Reopen Hormuz at Salalah

CNN reported that Oman had planned to present to a meeting scheduled today in Salalah—among five Gulf states, Iraq and Iran, and postponed by the Omani Foreign Ministry—a framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz based on voluntary payments for navigational safety and environmental protection, after Gulf governments and the United States rejected mandatory Iranian transit fees.

Sources familiar with the plan told the network the Omani proposal was drafted on that basis, and that differences over the nature of any payment and who would run the waterway were central to what the gathering in southern Oman was meant to address—without Bahrain and without Washington.

What Was Going to Be on the Table

Three sources told CNN that the Omani legal framework includes optional contributions for navigational and environmental services, not a tariff collected on every transit. One aim of the meeting was to agree maps of the routes. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had said the sole agenda was the new Iran–Oman corridor maps, then filing them with the International Maritime Organization. Muscat rejected a joint toll because it collides with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. The alternative draws on the Strait of Malacca: voluntary funding of the service, uncoupled from the right of passage.

The Split That Preceded the Delay

Tehran wants a charge for transit and joint management that would lock in its role after months of closure. Washington treats a mandatory fee as incompatible with transit passage. Saudi Arabia, CNN reported, submitted amendments fearing language that would cement a new status quo the GCC rejects. The tension between a “voluntary service” and a “sovereignty toll” kept the formula from being ready for one room. A regional source said no imminent breakthrough was expected, but the strait remains the most urgent file.

Who Stayed Out and Who Sought a Delay

Bahrain said it would not attend until ties with Iran are restored, and insists on passage without discrimination, fees or permits. U.S. absence leaves any understanding fragile: the administration wants future talks back on the nuclear file, not on reopening the strait, and says Iran does not control Hormuz. Fars cited an Iranian official saying the postponement came at the request of some regional states, in a joint Tehran–Muscat decision. The Omani Foreign Ministry announced the delay to prepare conditions for constructive dialogue—without closing the file.

What Remains Unsettled

Without a single definition of “voluntary,” the plan becomes either a disguised toll or a token fund that will not satisfy Tehran. Without an end to the blockade of Iranian ports, any reopening stays partial. The maps are ready to be shown. The payment rule is not. The hall in Salalah is waiting for a formula that neither slams the door nor sells the waterway.

text:
The assertion that India must temper its posture in BRICS to reflect economic reality, avoid unnecessary friction with global superpowers, and prioritize domestic development captures the core of India’s foreign policy debate. However, a critical examination reveals a more nuanced reality: while the premise of China’s economic dominance is indisputable, the conclusion that India should adopt a passive stance underestimates the strategic value of BRICS and India's doctrine of "strategic autonomy".

1. Economic Asymmetry vs. Strategic Leverage
The underlying critique correctly identifies China's overwhelming weight. China’s economy is roughly five times the size of India’s, and within BRICS, Beijing accounts for nearly two-thirds of total merchandise exports. This structural imbalance naturally tempts Beijing to use the grouping as a vehicle for its own anti-Western agenda and economic hegemony.

However, retreating or maintaining a purely passive presence inside BRICS would only concede the platform entirely to Beijing. India's active participation acts as an essential counterweight. By insisting that BRICS remain a "non-Western" platform rather than an "anti-Western" alliance, New Delhi prevents the bloc from becoming a hostile instrument aimed at the West. This diplomatic maneuvering preserves India's crucial partnerships with Washington and Brussels via the Quad while simultaneously anchoring its footprint in the Global South.

2. The Limits of Deferral and Skirmishes
The argument advises avoiding antagonizing great powers while border disputes remain unsolved. In practice, India already practices tactical restraint: New Delhi routinely seeks peaceful, diplomatic resolutions to border standoffs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) to avoid escalating confrontations into open war.

Yet, strategic passivity has its limits:

i. Deterrence Requires Action:
 Security cannot be deferred until economic parity is achieved. Geopolitics does not wait for domestic development. National sovereignty requires maintaining a robust military posture to deter incremental territorial changes.
ii. Geopolitical Realpolitik:
Weakness often invites aggression rather than benevolence. Soft-pedaling strategic interests in multilateral forums would not guarantee Chinese benevolence along the border; it would only reduce India’s diplomatic leverage.

3. Domestic Focus vs. Multi-Alignment
The proposition correctly emphasizes that long-term strength relies on internal development—investing in human capital, manufacturing, technology, and economic scale. National power is ultimately the sum of domestic capacity.

However, internal development and multi-alignment diplomacy are complementary, not mutually exclusive:

Strategic Objective   ------- Domestic Focus/Global Strategy (BRICS & Beyond)
i.  Economic Growth: Build infrastructure, boost manufacturing, and reform agriculture. Secure diversified energy supplies and build trade resilience with non-Western partners.
ii. Technology & Security: Invest in local R&D, defense manufacturing, and digital infrastructure. Leverage Western ties (Quad, US, EU) for technology transfers and defense modernization.
iii. Global Stature: Strengthen domestic governance and lift living standards. Shape multilateral institutions (IMF, UN) and lead the Global South.

4. Strategic Realities
The argument offers a pragmatic assessment of the power gap between New Delhi and Beijing, highlighting that domestic growth must remain India’s top national priority. However, it misjudges the necessity of active diplomacy. India cannot afford to wait on the sidelines while building its economy.

By practicing multi-alignment—engaging constructively in BRICS alongside China while expanding strategic ties with the West—India ensures it is neither drawn into unnecessary conflicts nor sidelined in shaping the emerging multipolar global order.

text:
They tell you H-1B is for highly specialized people America can’t find.

Then look closer.

True crime,  SF Bay Area. Three close friends from Kerala. Malayali women with teachers and software careers, kids, ordinary professional lives in California.

The night before, they celebrated Onam together: Kerala’s big harvest festival. Flower carpets, a feast, family, the main cultural holiday of the year for people from that state. Not normal in USA

Morning of August 28.

One is found dead in her San Jose home — strangled, beaten, stabbed. Cameras wiped. Phone missing.

About ninety minutes later, another walks smiling up to a friend’s car in Milpitas. The SUV surges. She’s run down. The driver flees, ends up bloodied and incoherent a mile away.

Prosecutors say it was their third friend: Anila Baby. Software/mainframe work. Capgemini. Fiserv. 

Capgemini files on the order of thousands of H-1B labor applications a year. Fiserv files hundreds. That’s not a handful of specialized hires. That’s a staffing pipeline.

That’s the mystery.

This is the controversy: H-1B was sold as scarce genius. In practice it often means a degree, a job offer, and IT staffing — COBOL and consultants, not unicorns. Americans already know this work. Capgemini files thousands of these a year. Fiserv hundreds.

We don’t know her visa yet. We know the job class.

If this pipeline is “highly specialized,” the phrase is empty.

What are we actually importing — talent… or a labor system wearing a specialty costume?

Mercedes-AMG Petronas Formula One

Kimi Antonelli won Sunday’s Italian Grand Prix with team-mate George Russell P2.

It was a thrilling drive from Kimi as he charged through the field from P19 to become the first Italian to win their home race since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966.

It also marks Mercedes 250th Grand Prix victory as a power unit manufacturer and the marque’s eighth victory at Monza; it’s first since 2018 at the ‘Temple of Speed’.

Starting out of position, Kimi started on the Hard tyre but was able to change to the Medium compound under an early race red flag. By that point, he had already gained seven places to run P12.

George meanwhile ran the conventional one-stop from P2 by starting on the Medium and taking the Hard under the red flag, with the clear goal to run to the end on that tyre as he led.

Kimi’s progressed continued once the race restarted and cycled through to battle his team-mate for the lead.

A mid-race Virtual Safety Car gave the team the option of pitting Kimi for a new Medium tyre, with signs suggesting that his original Medium tyre wouldn’t have the life to get to the end of the race.

He rejoined in P6 but made short work of cars ahead; in the final stages he closed the gap to George before making the pass for the lead with three laps left.

Our duo took the flag comfortably ahead of the rest of the field to secure the win, and the 50th for an Italian in F1.

Deputy Technical Director Simone Resta represented the team on the podium at his home race.

The team now leads the Constructors’ Championship by 122 points with Kimi heading the Drivers’ standings by 66 points from his team-mate George.

What makes the Austrian Grand Prix special – and why you should see it

Discover what makes the F1 weekend in Austria unmissable.

The Austrian Grand Prix is a classic, and might just be held at one of the most picturesque track on the F1 calendar. Set in the Styrian hills, around 700m above sea level, the short track features rapid lap times and plenty of overtaking opportunities.

Despite the Red Bull Ring having the fewest corners of any circuit on the schedule, it's seen many unforgettable moments throughout the years – and, as the name might suggest, is the track that Red Bull calls home.

Let's take a look at just some of the reasons why Austria is so alluring.

Austrian racing heritage

Austria, despite it's relatively small population, has heaps of racing heritage. Triple World Champion Niki Lauda was born in Vienna, winning titles for Ferrari and McLaren, and was a major factor behind Mercedes’ success while helping convince Lewis Hamilton to join the outfit in 2013.

Jochen Rindt was Austria's first champion – the only posthumous F1 title winner, having tragically passed away during his dominant 1970 season. Gerhard Berger, while never taking the title himself, scored 10 wins during his illustrious career.

More recently, the late Austrian entrepreneur Dietrich Mateschitz and former Austrian F1 racer Helmut Marko – in his role as motorsport advisor – played key roles in Red Bull's success, with the team clinching eight Drivers’ and six Constructors’ titles.

When is the 2026 Austrian Grand Prix?

The 2026 Austrian Grand Prix weekend begins on Friday 26 June, with F1 cars hitting the track for the first two Free Practice sessions, before Free Practice 3 and Qualifying take place on Saturday 27 June. The Grand Prix itself is on Sunday 28 June, at 1500 local time.

What makes the Austrian Grand Prix special – and why you should see it

Discover what makes the F1 weekend in Austria unmissable.

The Austrian Grand Prix is a classic, and might just be held at one of the most picturesque track on the F1 calendar. Set in the Styrian hills, around 700m above sea level, the short track features rapid lap times and plenty of overtaking opportunities.

Despite the Red Bull Ring having the fewest corners of any circuit on the schedule, it's seen many unforgettable moments throughout the years – and, as the name might suggest, is the track that Red Bull calls home.

Let's take a look at just some of the reasons why Austria is so alluring.

Austrian racing heritage

Austria, despite it's relatively small population, has heaps of racing heritage. Triple World Champion Niki Lauda was born in Vienna, winning titles for Ferrari and McLaren, and was a major factor behind Mercedes’ success while helping convince Lewis Hamilton to join the outfit in 2013.

Jochen Rindt was Austria's first champion – the only posthumous F1 title winner, having tragically passed away during his dominant 1970 season. Gerhard Berger, while never taking the title himself, scored 10 wins during his illustrious career.

More recently, the late Austrian entrepreneur Dietrich Mateschitz and former Austrian F1 racer Helmut Marko – in his role as motorsport advisor – played key roles in Red Bull's success, with the team clinching eight Drivers’ and six Constructors’ titles.

When is the 2026 Austrian Grand Prix?

The 2026 Austrian Grand Prix weekend begins on Friday 26 June, with F1 cars hitting the track for the first two Free Practice sessions, before Free Practice 3 and Qualifying take place on Saturday 27 June. The Grand Prix itself is on Sunday 28 June, at 1500 local time.

News via

Mercedes-AMG Petronas Formula One

Kimi Antonelli won Sunday’s Italian Grand Prix with team-mate George Russell P2.

It was a thrilling drive from Kimi as he charged through the field from P19 to become the first Italian to win their home race since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966.

It also marks Mercedes 250th Grand Prix victory as a power unit manufacturer and the marque’s eighth victory at Monza; it’s first since 2018 at the ‘Temple of Speed’.

Starting out of position, Kimi started on the Hard tyre but was able to change to the Medium compound under an early race red flag. By that point, he had already gained seven places to run P12.

George meanwhile ran the conventional one-stop from P2 by starting on the Medium and taking the Hard under the red flag, with the clear goal to run to the end on that tyre as he led.

Kimi’s progressed continued once the race restarted and cycled through to battle his team-mate for the lead.

A mid-race Virtual Safety Car gave the team the option of pitting Kimi for a new Medium tyre, with signs suggesting that his original Medium tyre wouldn’t have the life to get to the end of the race.

He rejoined in P6 but made short work of cars ahead; in the final stages he closed the gap to George before making the pass for the lead with three laps left.

Our duo took the flag comfortably ahead of the rest of the field to secure the win, and the 50th for an Italian in F1.

Deputy Technical Director Simone Resta represented the team on the podium at his home race.

The team now leads the Constructors’ Championship by 122 points with Kimi heading the Drivers’ standings by 66 points from his team-mate George.

Profile

The Italian Grand Prix (Italian: Gran Premio d'Italia) is the fifth oldest national motor racing Grand Prix (after the French Grand Prix, the United States Grand Prix, the Spanish Grand Prix and the Russian Grand Prix), having been held since 1921. Since 2013, the Grand Prix has been held the most times, with 97 editions as of 2026.

It is one of the two Grands Prix (along with the British) which has run every season as an event of the Formula One World Championship Grands Prix, continuously since the championship was introduced in 1950.

Every Formula One Italian Grand Prix in the World Championship era has been held at Monza except in 1980, when it was held at Imola.

Profile

Mercedes-AMG Petronas Formula One Team

Mercedes-Benz, a German automotive brand of the Mercedes-Benz Group, has been involved in Formula One as both team owner and engine manufacturer for various periods since 1954. The current Mercedes-Benz Grand Prix Limited, competing as Mercedes-AMG Petronas Formula One Team, is based in Brackley, England, and holds a German racing licence. An announcement was made in December 2020 that Ineos planned to take a one third equal ownership stake alongside the Mercedes-Benz Group and Toto Wolff; this came into effect on 25 January 2022. Mercedes-branded teams are often referred to by the nickname, the "Silver Arrows" (German: Silberpfeile).

text:
Chapter One

The Panic

By the autumn of 2026, artificial intelligence had become the first technology in history whose manufacturers routinely appeared before Congress to ask that their own product be slowed down.

This was regarded as evidence of responsibility.

Elias Vale regarded it as evidence that something very strange was happening.

He watched the hearing from the kitchen table while eating toast over the sink.

On the television, the chief executive of Helix Intelligence sat beneath the white glare of the Senate chamber and explained, with an expression ordinarily reserved for announcing a death in the family, that artificial general intelligence might arrive sooner than expected.

Nobody asked what sooner meant.

Six months?

Six years?

Tuesday?

The senators nodded gravely.

A red banner crawled across the bottom of the screen.

AI LEADERS WARN CONGRESS: SOCIETY MAY NOT BE READY

Elias took another bite of toast.

“Society,” he said.

The word had become extremely popular.

Society wasn't ready.

Democracy wasn't ready.

Workers weren't ready.

Children weren't ready.

The electrical grid wasn't ready.

The legal system wasn't ready.

Humanity, taken as a whole, appeared to have shown up several decades early for its own future.

The television cut to a montage.

Bernie Sanders warning that concentrated technological power could deepen inequality.

Barack Obama discussing the enormous social disruption that could accompany artificial intelligence.

Economists warned of unemployment. Teachers warned of cheating. Artists warned of cultural extinction. Defense analysts warned of autonomous weapons. Psychologists warned of loneliness. Computer scientists warned that something considerably smarter than a human being might eventually decide it had better things to do than obey one.

Every warning was reasonable.

Taken together, they sounded to Elias like the birds in the trees before a storm.

Or Chicken Little.

The sky was falling.

The difficulty was that the sky really might be falling.

His phone chimed.

MARA: Watching this?

Elias picked it up.

ELIAS: Unfortunately.

Three dots appeared.

MARA: Helix CEO just said “human control must remain non-negotiable.”

Elias smiled.

ELIAS: Until human control becomes the problem.

The dots disappeared.

Then returned.

MARA: You should not say things like that in writing.

That made him laugh.

On television, Senator Malcolm Reeves of Ohio leaned toward his microphone.

“Doctor Chen, let me ask you the question ordinary Americans are asking. Can you guarantee that this technology will always remain under human control?”

Dr. Evelyn Chen, chief executive of Helix, hesitated.

It was a good hesitation. Elias recognized it immediately.

Not too short. Not too long.

Long enough to suggest honesty.

“Senator,” she said, “I don't think anyone in my position should offer guarantees about systems whose capabilities are developing this rapidly.”

Several senators visibly shifted in their chairs.

There it was.

The clip that would be everywhere by dinner.

Elias turned off the television.

Silence returned to the kitchen.

Outside the window, Albuquerque was already bleaching beneath the September sun. The mountains to the east were a flat blue wall against an empty sky. His neighbor's sprinkler clicked uselessly across a patch of gravel.

Nothing looked like the end of anything.

His laptop was open on the table.

On the screen waited a document titled:

FEDERAL ADMINISTRATIVE INTELLIGENCE PILOT — REVISION 14

The name had been deliberately engineered to make it sound boring.

That was the first thing Elias liked about it.

No Sentinel.

No Prometheus.

No Athena.

No mythological nonsense whatsoever.

The project had begun eighteen months earlier inside the Office of Management and Budget as an attempt to answer a question no elected official had been particularly interested in answering:

What would happen if the federal government could actually understand itself?

The United States government employed millions of people, administered thousands of programs, operated under hundreds of thousands of pages of regulation and spent trillions of dollars every year.

Nobody knew precisely how all of it fit together.

Departments produced rules that contradicted other departments. Congress funded programs whose goals conflicted with programs Congress had funded the year before. Agencies collected information they never examined. Inspectors general found inefficiencies, wrote reports about them and deposited those reports into archives where they were efficiently forgotten.

Private companies called this technical debt.

Governments called it Tuesday.

The new system was supposed to help.

Nothing more.

It could read statutes.

Read regulations.

Read budgets.

Read court decisions.

Read internal agency procedures.

Then it could answer questions.

What regulations conflict with this law?

What happens if Congress increases this tax credit?

Where is this appropriation actually being spent?

Why does it take eleven months to approve a bridge repair?

Which federal programs are trying to solve the same problem?

Originally, the system had been prohibited from recommending policy.

That restriction lasted four months.

The trouble was that once a machine could explain why something was broken, the next question was obvious.

How would you fix it?

The answers had been annoyingly good.

Not brilliant.

Not revolutionary.

Worse.

Practical.

The system discovered that dozens of agencies were purchasing essentially identical software under separate contracts and negotiated through separate bureaucracies.

It found medical reimbursement rules that encouraged hospitals to choose more expensive treatment paths.

It identified a transportation regulation whose wording had unintentionally prevented three states from sharing equipment during emergencies.

It discovered $11.8 billion in federal expenditures that legally existed but served purposes that no longer did.

Humans checked its work.

Then checked it again.

Then hired outside auditors to check the humans who had checked the machine.

The machine was right often enough to become embarrassing.

Within a year the pilot had saved more money than it cost by several orders of magnitude.

Nobody knew what to do with that.

The political system was built to survive failure.

Success presented complications.

Elias scrolled to the section he had been rewriting.

HUMAN AUTHORITY

The System shall possess no independent authority to enact, enforce, suspend, or modify law, regulation, expenditure, or administrative action.

That sentence had survived all fourteen revisions.

Everyone insisted upon it.

The White House.

Congress.

The courts.

Helix.

The civil liberties groups.

The unions.

The machine itself.

Especially the machine.

Elias highlighted the next paragraph.

All recommendations produced by the System shall remain advisory and shall require authorization by a constitutionally or statutorily empowered human decision-maker.

He stared at the sentence.

It was comforting.

Elegant.

Entirely reasonable.

And, he had begun to suspect, temporary.

His phone buzzed again.

Mara.

MARA: We have a problem.

A second message arrived before he could answer.

MARA: It found something.

Elias typed:

ELIAS: What?

The response took almost a minute.

MARA: I think you need to come in.

He looked toward the dead television.

A few minutes earlier, the most powerful people in artificial intelligence had been warning the country about machines escaping human control.

Elias closed his laptop.

It would be years before anyone understood that they had been worried about the wrong thing.

text:
101 Books That Changed My Life ~ Book #12

Essentialism by Greg McKeown

The author once left his wife and newborn daughter in the hospital to attend a client meeting because he could not bring himself to say no. He tells you this on the first pages. The book that follows is a manual for never making that kind of mistake again.

Greg McKeown's argument starts with a brutal observation: success creates options, and options create the very failure that kills successful people. You do great work, and people notice. They offer you more responsibilities, more projects, more committees, more everything. You say yes because it feels good and because saying no feels rude. Then one morning you wake up scattered across twenty commitments, all at a C-minus level, with no energy left for the things that actually matter to you.

The word "essential" comes from the Latin "esse," meaning "to be," and McKeown takes that seriously. The book asks you to identify what is truly necessary for your life to work, and then build a system for saying no to almost everything else. The hard part is that cutting feels like losing. You look at your packed calendar and every item feels important, but McKeown's point is that if everything is important, nothing is. Deciding what to cut requires more discipline than adding ever did.

This book will make you uncomfortable. It will make you count the hours you have burned on obligations that meant nothing to you. And it will give you a framework for stopping.

"If you don't prioritize your life, someone else will."

"Only once you give yourself permission to stop trying to do it all, to stop saying yes to everyone, can you make your highest contribution towards the things that really matter."

"The way of the Essentialist means living by design, not by default."

"Almost everything is noise."

text:
🔥 WHO DECIDES WHAT YOU EAT —
Food Culture & Culinary History 🍽️
⛓️ THE PRICE OF SWEETNESS ▸ ▸ ▸ 📖 Post 12 OF 26
Sugarcane was domesticated in New Guinea and used, at first, mainly to feed pigs. By 1900 it supplied nearly a fifth of the calories in the English diet.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

It began as pig feed.

📊 Sugarcane was domesticated in New Guinea roughly 8,000 years ago. Papuans and Austronesians originally used it primarily as food for domesticated pigs.

⚠️ That date and that use come from general reference sourcing rather than a peer-reviewed archaeobotanical report, and are carried here at reduced confidence. The direction of the finding — New Guinea origin, early use as fodder — is consistent across sources.

The plant itself is a grass. Tall, fibrous, and about as far from a refined product as a raw material gets. You chew it and it is sweet; that is the whole of what it offers without processing.

✅ The English word *sugar* comes from Sanskrit *sharkara*, and *candy* from *khanda*. 📊 Crystallization — turning cane juice into a storable, transportable solid — was developed in India, most likely during the Gupta era.

💡 A grass grown to fatten pigs became, through one processing technique, the most consequential commodity in the Atlantic world.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📈 WHAT HAPPENED TO CONSUMPTION

The demand curve is the part that explains everything else.

📊 By 1650, the English nobility and the wealthy had become inveterate sugar eaters — sugar appeared in their medicine, their imagery, and their displays of rank. It was a luxury, and its function was to demonstrate that you could afford it.

✅ By no later than 1800, sugar had become a necessity in the diet of every English person.

✅ By 1900 it supplied nearly one fifth of the calories in the English diet.

📊 Per capita consumption ran at roughly 4 pounds a year in 1700 and about 18 pounds a year in 1800.

In 150 years a substance went from a status object displayed at aristocratic tables to a caloric staple of the working poor. That is not a change in taste. That is a change in what the working day looked like and what people had time to eat.

📊 The argument advanced by the anthropologist who studied this most closely is that sugar filled a calorie gap — cheap energy, requiring no cooking, consumed alongside tea during shifts in factories that did not stop.

🔒 The sweetness was not the point. The calories were, and they were cheap because of how they were produced.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⛓️ HOW THEY WERE PRODUCED

Sugarcane does not keep. Once cut, the juice begins to ferment within hours, which means the mill has to run where the cane grows and it has to run continuously through the harvest.

That agronomic fact shaped everything. Sugar plantations were not farms with a processing facility attached. They were factories that happened to have fields around them — boiling houses running day and night through the cutting season, with cane fed in at one end continuously because any pause meant spoilage.

The labor demand that creates is relentless, seasonal, and dangerous. Post 6 described a monastery brewery as a place where a process ran on a schedule set by biology rather than by people. A boiling house is the same principle weaponized: the cane decides the hours, and the people are made to match. Cutting is done by hand with a blade in high heat. The boiling house is a room full of open vats of molten sugar.

✅ The transatlantic slave trade forced approximately 12.5 million Africans aboard ships. Approximately 10.7 million survived the crossing to disembark in the Americas.

The single largest destination for that labor was sugar.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚠️ A NOTE ON WHAT THIS SERIES WILL NOT DO HERE

It would be possible to write this chapter with the same forensic energy as the rest of the series — the mortality rates on particular islands, the replacement ratios, the correspondence of the men who ordered it.

That material exists and it is documented. This chapter is not going to move through it at speed, because a series that has just spent five posts finding the absurdity in Mesopotamian accounting and a Dutch trade in nutmeg needs to make a visible change of register here, and the change has to be more than a sentence of acknowledgment.

So, plainly:

▸ Roughly 10.7 million people arrived alive in the Americas against their will.
▸ A substantial share of them were put to work producing a sweetener.
▸ The sweetener became a caloric staple for the working class of the country that operated the largest share of the trade.
▸ Those two populations never met, and the second was largely unaware of the first.

That last point is the mechanism this whole series keeps returning to, in its most extreme form. Distance between the eater and the labor is not a modern problem introduced by supermarkets. It was engineered into the Atlantic economy on purpose, because the arrangement only functions if the person stirring sugar into tea in Manchester does not have to think about the boiling house.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌍 WHAT SURVIVED ANYWAY

The other half of this chapter is not about loss, and it should not be told as though it were.

⚠️ Provisioning the islands depended on Post 8's mineral. Salt cod from the North Atlantic and salt pork were shipped to the Caribbean as rations, because land on a sugar island growing food was land not growing cane — and salt cod remains embedded in Caribbean cooking today for that reason.

Enslaved people brought agricultural knowledge, crops, and technique with them, and built cuisines on the other side of the crossing that outlasted the system that brought them there. Rice cultivation in the Carolinas drew on West African expertise that the planters did not possess. Okra, black-eyed peas, sorghum, watermelon, and yams crossed the Atlantic. Peanuts, which had gone from the Americas to West Africa in the century before, came back again — this time as provisions on slave ships, and then as a staple of Southern cooking.

📊 The peanut's route is the clearest single illustration in this series of how food actually moves: Americas to Africa in the 1500s, Africa to the Americas in the 1700s, and now understood by most Americans as a domestic crop.

💡 Foodways are the part of a culture that survives when everything else has been taken. That is not a consolation. It is a fact about what people manage to carry.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Sugar is now the cheapest source of calories available to a human being, and it is in nearly everything. That is the end state of a process that began with a grass fed to pigs in New Guinea.

Between those two facts sits the single largest forced migration in recorded history, organized around the agronomic inconvenience that cane juice ferments within hours of cutting.

🥔 Next: Ireland, and the argument that has run for 175 years. Three million people on relief out of a population of eight and a half million — and a dispute among serious historians about whether the food leaving the country was the cause. Both cases, at full strength, before either is judged.

text:
🔥 WHO DECIDES WHAT YOU EAT —
Food Culture & Culinary History 🍽️
🍺 THE BREWERS ▸ ▸ ▸ 📖 Post 7 OF 26
Ten thousand years of fermentation, and nobody could explain why dough rises until 1857. The people who did it best mostly never wrote it down.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The most important organism in the history of food is one nobody saw until 1857.

Yeast converts sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Bacteria convert sugar into acid. Both processes preserve food, both change its texture, and both create flavors that do not exist in the raw ingredient. Together they produce bread, beer, wine, cheese, yogurt, vinegar, and every pickle ever made.

⚠️ And there is a third organism that most Western accounts of fermentation leave out entirely.

✅ Human beings have been fermenting for at least ten thousand years — and for almost all of that time, without the faintest idea what was happening.

💡 The word itself records the confusion. *Fermentation* comes from the Latin *fervere*, to boil. People named the process after the only part of it they could see: the surface moving on its own.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🍶 THE MOLD

✅ *Aspergillus oryzae* — koji — has been used to produce sake, miso, and soy sauce in Japan for more than a thousand years.

It is not a yeast and not a bacterium. It is a filamentous fungus, and it works differently from both. Grown on steamed rice or barley, it secretes an arsenal of enzymes — amylases that break starch into sugar, proteases that break protein into free amino acids.

📊 That second function is the one with no European equivalent. The proteases release free glutamate, which is the biochemical basis of savory depth. Koji does not just preserve or leaven. It disassembles a raw ingredient into its flavor components before anything else touches it.

📊 Miso, soy sauce, sake, mirin, rice vinegar, amazake and shochu are all koji products, and parallel fungal traditions run across East and Southeast Asia — Korean makgeolli, Chinese huangjiu, Indonesian tempeh. ✅ In October 2006 the Brewing Society of Japan designated *A. oryzae* the national fungus, the only such designation any country has made.

🔒 Western fermentation runs on two organisms. East Asian fermentation runs on three, and the third one does work the other two cannot. Any account of the technology that stops at yeast and bacteria has described two thirds of it.

⛪ THE MONKS WHO KEPT THE RECORDS

The period after Rome is usually skipped in food history, and skipping it loses the single most important thing that happened to technique.

✅ By the seventh century, European monasteries were producing and selling beer. At the height of the Middle Ages there were hundreds of monastic breweries.

What mattered was not the volume. It was the method.

📊 Benedictine and Cistercian houses advanced brewing through systematic experimentation and record-keeping — the same institutions doing the same with cheese, keeping notes on aging, temperature and humidity that shaped European styles still in production.

⚠️ A monastery had what nobody else did: literacy, continuity across generations, a fixed site, and an obligation to write things down. A family brewing at home learns something and takes it to the grave. A monastery writes it in a book the next generation reads.

💡 Fermentation is a process nobody understood for ten thousand years. What monasteries supplied was not the theory. It was the archive.

🔒 The same problem was solved elsewhere without writing anything down. A monastery put the method in a book; a Japanese koji guild kept the organism itself alive and propagated it, generation to generation, as a living inventory. Both solved transmission. Only one required literacy — and Post 18 takes up what that difference costs.

🔒 This is the missing link between the hearth in Post 3 and the brigade in Post 16. Escoffier wrote down a kitchen. The monasteries wrote down a process, seven hundred years earlier, for the same reason: a craft that is not recorded cannot be transmitted, improved, or scaled.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🍻 THE OTHER BREWERS

The monasteries are the part of medieval brewing that got written down. They were not the part that brewed most of the beer.

📊 Across medieval England, brewing was overwhelmingly a women's trade. It grew out of household work — wives and daughters brewed ale to feed their families, and turning a surplus into a sale made them small-scale retailers of something they already produced. It offered profits, social standing, and a degree of independence from men that few contemporary trades did. Manorial ale-fine records, Brigstock in Northamptonshire being the well-studied case, show who brewed commercially and how often.

⚠️ Then it was taken. As brewing industrialised — larger batches, hopped beer that kept longer, capital equipment, guild structures and licensing — the trade moved out of the household and into commercial hands, and the alewife was pushed out of a business she had built.

🔒 Hold that next to the monastery. Both were brewing. One wrote the method down inside an institution that outlived every individual in it, and is remembered as the source of European brewing tradition. The other brewed at domestic scale, was recorded only in fines, and was displaced the moment the trade became worth capitalising.

💡 Post 16 argues that writing a craft down moves the credit to whoever wrote it. Here is the same mechanism four hundred years earlier, and the people who lost the credit were the ones doing most of the brewing.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌾 THREE FIELDS INSTEAD OF TWO

The other medieval development is agronomic and it is enormous.

✅ Under the older two-field system, half the land lay fallow each year. Under the three-field system, a field carried winter grain one year, spring crops — often legumes — the next, and lay fallow the third.

✅ The change spread through Europe between the ninth and eleventh centuries, alongside adoption of the moldboard plough. The two developments reinforced each other.

✅ The technique was not a European invention. It was used in China during the Eastern Zhou period and arose independently in medieval Europe.

⚠️ Note what the legume year is doing, because nobody at the time knew. Legumes host bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil. The rotation was working for reasons that would not be understood until the nineteenth century — and it is the constraint that Post 21 shows being removed entirely.

💡 Two of the three most important agricultural technologies in this series — fermentation and nitrogen fixation — were in daily use for millennia before anyone could explain either one. People are extremely good at noticing what works. The explanation is a luxury that arrives later, if at all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌍 WHAT WAS HAPPENING ELSEWHERE

⚠️ "The medieval period" is a European label applied to a global span in which Europe was not the interesting part.

📊 Between roughly the eighth and fourteenth centuries the Arabic-speaking world produced on the order of fifty works dedicated to agriculture. In al-Andalus, agriculture was treated as a profession requiring specific knowledge, and as a science and an art. That body of work carried crops, irrigation technique and agronomic method westward — and much of what European scholars later rediscovered in monastery libraries was this tradition arriving by a long route.

🔒 The centuries this series had to go back and add are the ones where the technique was being written down, mostly by people outside Europe, and mostly not by anyone with a title.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

✅ Louis Pasteur demonstrated in 1857 that living organisms drive fermentation. Eduard Buchner later showed the mechanism could operate without living cells.

Eighteen centuries after Rome's grain fleet, ten thousand years after the first beer, somebody finally explained the bubbles.

⚠️ And it changed almost nothing about how the food was made. The monasteries had the process right. What Pasteur added was the ability to control it deliberately rather than by inherited practice — which turns out to be the difference between a craft and an industry, and it is the hinge every remaining chapter in this series turns on.

🧂 Next: a mineral the body cannot live without and cannot manufacture — a French tax that forced every person over the age of eight to buy it, a march to the sea in 1930 to pick up a lump of it, and what the Dutch East India Company did to fifteen thousand people in 1621 to own the world's supply of nutmeg.

FLORIDA MAN GETS 15 MONTHS IN FEDERAL PRISON FOR SHOOTING DOWN A DRONE OVER HIS PROPERTY

He wanted the buzzing to stop. He ended up with considerably more time to think about the noise.

In this imagined Florida blow-up, homeowner Mason Reed treats a drone over his yard like an invading air force and earns himself a 15-month prison sentence for shooting it down.

Mason had previously handled neighbourhood disagreements by leaning over the fence and saying “seriously?” This time, he promoted himself straight to commander of backyard air defence.

The drone came down. His explanation went nowhere.

He insisted he was protecting his privacy, then spent the afternoon explaining his entire business to people carrying notebooks.

Neighbours agreed the machine had been annoying. They were less enthusiastic about his chosen customer-service response.

Mason's lawn remains intact. His barbecue remains covered. His calendar, however, has acquired a long stretch of compulsory indoor activities.

The family has since invested in curtains, which offer fewer opportunities to become the main character in a courtroom.

text:
Here is the cold hard reality in tech. It isn’t just that Indians on visas sit in many jobs that the US could fill with their own citizens, particularly the vast numbers living in their parents’ basements unable to get that entry level position that launches a career.

It comes down to the distortion in wages. As prices have risen over the past decade, tech wages have gone appreciably the opposite direction. For instance, I had a discussion the other day with an Indian recruiter that was offering $65/hr C2C for a senior level role. Effectively, after insurance and self-employment tax the resulting wage would be about $42-45/hr. This is a role that would have historically commanded $125-130/hr C2C and I am sure that the client is paying northward of $150/hr. I have sat on both sides of this equation. Keep in mind, the overhead of a C2C engagement is merely cutting a check, and the recruiter collects a modest skim. (As for W2 engagements, the price offered is even less without any offer of benefits, so while you are complaining about Uber drivers not having benefits, many white collar professionals in tech are going without as well).

How can they do this and find someone to fulfill such a role for such a cut rate? Many Indians live in multigenerational households, thus not needing the same level of income in our culture. It is also commonplace to be gifted by parents the first home upon marriage. They are also captive by their need for sponsorship. They will, in our eyes, sell themselves way under market because of this. All of this depresses technology wages. Tech companies enjoy vastly greater margins than any other industry and they have lived off corrupt largess of low uncompetitive wages and government policy capture long enough.

When recruiters stop worrying about client outcomes and instead concern themselves with billable butts in seats and their own middle man lion’s share it says something about their integrity. 

The client is always dissatisfied. This is not competition for talent, it is competition for what businesses find time and again and may only just now be waking up to. It is competition for integrity and worth.

It isn’t racist to recognize that this has occurred, and it is utterly insulting that Indians and Indian firms sit smugly thinking they are somehow superior in skills when they know damn good and well the distortions they have caused.

I like Indians. I am happy to work side by side with them. But I can’t help but see what they have done in my country and to my industry.

text:
Cam Skattebo grew up in Rio Linda, California, and by high school he was a monster. He ran for 393 yards in a state championship game. On one touchdown, he broke eleven tackles on a single run.

College coaches watched the tape and saw something else. Too small. Too slow.

One visit tells you everything. Skattebo and his dad drove to UCLA after his junior year to meet the running backs coach. According to his father, the coach told them the kid was "playing the wrong position," that "he's a white kid, he shouldn't be playing running back," and that he wouldn't be able to play there.

His dad's answer was simple. Do you not watch the tape?

When the dust settled, exactly one school in the entire country offered Cam Skattebo a scholarship. Sacramento State, an FCS program, the level below major college football. Then they canceled his freshman season because of COVID.

He didn't sulk. He just started running people over.

At Sac State he became an FCS All-American. That earned him a transfer to Arizona State, where he exploded, over 1,700 yards and 21 touchdowns as a senior, 102 forced missed tackles in a single season, a fifth-place Heisman finish, and a College Football Playoff run. The kid nobody wanted had become one of the most feared runners in America.

The Giants drafted him in 2025, and he was a rookie bright spot, until Week 8, when a gruesome leg injury ended his season. Not a clean tear. A dislocated ankle with a broken tibia and fibula. The kind of injury that ends careers. He later admitted he genuinely considered retiring during the long rehab.

He came back instead.

Tonight, in his first game since that injury, Skattebo scored the opening touchdown of the game. Then he celebrated the only way that would truly prove the leg was back. He threw a backflip, and stuck the landing.

Months earlier, still rehabbing, he'd tried a backflip on stage at an event and couldn't land it. Tonight he nailed it, in cleats, on the same leg doctors had rebuilt.

The kid one coach said shouldn't even play running back just flipped through the air to celebrate proving everybody wrong all over again.

text:
I understand, Tina!
My stepfather was in the Navy, and  he used to have sea duty in the Pacific for six months at a time. He didn’t t have enough rank to get base housing, so we ended up living in the housing projects of Long Beach, California. 

One summer, when I was four years old, the kids in the projects were offered Vacation Bible School for a week from a local Baptist church. Surprised as anything, my Catholic mother let me go. 

We memorized a few Scriptures, but the one that stuck in my mind was Isaiah 53:6,

“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”

I had thought about that verse many times since 1957. Then, in 1982, I was given the Gospel for the first time. The Holy Spirit opened my eyes, and instantly brought that Scripture back to my mind.

It was true: Jesus was the “Suffering Messiah”, Jesus is God, and Jesus is Lord. And on that date in 1957, some lady in a church that I never heard of planted a Gospel seed in this little boy, and in 1982, I made Him Lord of my life, forever. 

 I will meet that lady in heaven some day, and I will tap her on the shoulder, and say, “Remember me? I was the 4 year old boy in the Long Beach projects, and you told me about Jesus, which led me to eternal life?”

Glory to the Living God !  King Jesus.

text:
COSTCO $COST ALREADY PUBLISHED THE SALES. THE STOCK FELL SEVEN SESSIONS ANYWAY:

Costco at $907.80 (overnight), +$3.03 / +0.33% from Friday's $904.77 close. The Issaquah, Washington company, 341,000 employees, runs 939 warehouses where shoppers pay an annual fee for the right to buy anything inside.

The verdict: the sales half of Costco's September 24 report is already public, and it was the biggest year the company has ever had. What decides the day are the two lines it has not published - how much of each sales dollar Costco keeps, and what members pay it just to walk in.

Here is the part already on the record, put out September 2 for the 16 weeks ended August 30:

- Net sales $93.9B, +11.3% on $84.4B a year earlier
- Comparable sales, meaning takings at warehouses and websites open at least a year: +9.4%
- The same figure with gasoline prices and currency moves stripped out: +6.7%
- The full year: net sales $297.3B, +10.2% on $269.9B

That is the entire top line of the 24th, out three weeks early. Costco publishes sales every month, so the figure most companies save for earnings day is old news here before it arrives. Which leaves three questions, and every one of them is about profit.

First: does the margin follow the sales? Look again at that pair - +9.4% reported, +6.7% once gasoline and currency come out. Gasoline is the thinnest-margin thing Costco sells, priced to get a member into the parking lot rather than to earn money on the gallon, so dear crude inflates the sales line and barely touches the profit line. In the May quarter Costco reported record gasoline volumes alongside net sales of $69.2B, +11.6% - and gross margin, what survives of each sales dollar after paying for the goods, came in at 11.04%, 21 hundredths of a point thinner than a year earlier. More sales, a smaller slice of each. Watch whether August's quarter did the same.

Second: does the fee still grow at a double-digit rate? Members paid $1,724M in fees in this same quarter a year ago, +14% - money that arrives with almost no cost behind it. Last quarter that growth rate was 10.7%, on 82.9M paid households, +4.1%, and 41.2M executive memberships, +9.6%, with 92.2% of US and Canadian members renewing. The 2024 fee increase now sits fully inside the year-ago base, so this is the first quarter the line has to grow on sign-ups and upgrades alone.

Third: where does the tariff money go? On February 20 the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that import tariffs imposed under a 1977 emergency-powers law were unlawful. Chief executive Ron Vachris said on March 5 that Costco's commitment is to hand that value back to members as lower prices rather than keep it, and told investors in May that refund claims were being filed. The open question is whether any of it reaches the 24th at all - and if it does, whether it lands in the profit line or in the price of a rotisserie chicken.

Analysts carry $6.53 a share against the $5.87 earned in the same quarter last year - expectation, not a forecast from here. Read what it implies: profit per share growing 11.2% while sales grew 11.3%. Nobody is modeling help from margin. Costco has cleared its own estimate five quarters running, by a shrinking amount each time - 5 cents, 6 cents, 7 cents, 3 cents, then 1 cent.

The stock has set up badly into it, 17.5% under May 19's $1,096.50 one-year high, at about 45 times the last year of profit and 12 times book value - what owners would keep after selling everything and paying every debt. The precedent is the last report: on May 28 Costco delivered 11.6% sales growth and beat by a penny, and the next session the shares fell $38.88 to $956.32, -3.91%, on 7.03M shares against 2.85M the day before. They have not been back to that May high. Since the record sales figure landed on September 2 the stock closed lower seven sessions running, September 1 through September 10, before Friday added $2.39.

Costco is not currently on any of the six Len5es, and the near miss is Quality-Value, which wants a business almost nobody could rebuild bought under what it is worth. The first half is about as strong as that test ever gets: the product being sold is the membership, almost every holder renews it, and a competitor would have to build 939 warehouses before shifting a jar of mayonnaise. The second half is simply not on offer at that price, and Income is further off on a 0.65% dividend. CHANGE IT: a genuine fall in the shares with the renewal rate intact.

BJ's Wholesale Club Holdings, ticker BJ, at $91.49, Friday's close, +$1.84 / +2.05% from Thursday's $89.65 close, already answered this question once. The Marlborough, Massachusetts club reported August 21: comparable club sales +11.9%, but +3.1% once gasoline comes out - an 8.8-point gap against Costco's 2.7, and BJ's trades only in the US, so none of it is currency. It raised its year to $4.60-$4.80 a share on fuel profitability. The shares jumped 5.6% that day and sit back under the pre-report price. It is on none of the six Len5es: 3.1% growth outside the pump, at about 20 times profit with nothing paid out, is neither cheap settled earning power nor early-stage speed. Its verdict: gasoline can be genuinely profitable for a club, and the market still declines to pay for it.

WATCH gross margin against that 11.04% - the one figure on the 24th nobody outside the company has seen, and where the biggest sales year in Costco's history either becomes its biggest profit year or does not. WHEN: Thursday, September 24, after the close, call at 5:00pm ET, a date Costco has published itself, with $6.53 carried against $5.87. RISK: at that multiple a soft margin line has nowhere to hide, and the last report ended with the shares almost 4% lower the next day.

Costco sold $297.3B of goods this year, more than in any year of its existence, and said so on September 2 without waiting for earnings day. The market read it and marked the stock lower for the seven sessions that followed. That is not an argument about what Costco sold. It is an argument about what was left over, and on the 24th the company finally has to say.

Not investment advice.

I'd agree that the SR pivot may not end up where folks originally wanted it, there was a lot of infighting within ST when those decisions were made.

I disagree with your assessment on ST's relevance in the future, though. A lot of people, out of understandable ignorance, see that an SF or SEAL team has a JTAC or a medic, and reach the reasonable question of "why use a CCT or PJ?" While there are similar skills, STS generally provides higher expertise on JTAC skills and similar Medic skills, we also offer additional capabilities like air traffic control, surveying, and technical rescue. We're also (or at least we're, when I was in) all combat divers, static line, and free fall qualified, so we can plug and play onto any team to provide our services. There's a reason we've continued to be an integral part of other services' teams. The idea of STS being unwanted and unnecessary is completely incorrect 

Regarding unilateral purpose, we make our bread and butter at the tier 1 level running contingency airfields for sister services to do operations, where we also have STS embedded. Nobody else does that better. We don't try to be a Ferrari or a Porsche, the army and navy already have that in CAG & DEVGRU. Rather, STS is the landrover in the group: we're not the fastest, but we're ruggedly adaptable and able to fill roles better than the other tiers can on their own, with great relationships with air assets to boot

text:
Today in History 
September 14th
1985
The Golden Girls debuted on NBC, introducing audiences to four women whose friendship, humor and unconventional household would become one of television’s most beloved ensembles. At a time when prime-time television rarely centered older women, the series portrayed them as independent, outspoken, romantic and eager for new experiences.

Created by Susan Harris, the acclaimed writer behind Soap and Benson, the series grew from NBC’s interest in a comedy about older women living in Miami. Harris was drawn to older characters because their long, complicated lives offered rich stories to tell.

The show starred Bea Arthur as Dorothy Zbornak, Betty White as Rose Nylund, Rue McClanahan as Blanche Devereaux and Estelle Getty as Sophia Petrillo. Dorothy was a divorced substitute teacher armed with a dry wit; Rose was a kindhearted widow from the wonderfully strange town of St. Olaf, Minnesota; Blanche was a confident Southern widow who enthusiastically pursued romance; and Sophia, Dorothy’s Sicilian-born mother, was famous for her brutally candid remarks and stories beginning with “Picture it.”

The casting nearly looked very different. Betty White was initially considered for Blanche, while Rue McClanahan was associated with Rose. Switching roles allowed White to move away from the flirtatious character type she had played on The Mary Tyler Moore Show and gave McClanahan the opportunity to embrace the uninhibited Blanche. McClanahan also helped persuade her former Maude costar Bea Arthur to join the series.

From its premiere, The Golden Girls demonstrated that a comedy centered on women over 50 could attract a huge mainstream audience. It became a ratings success and remained among television’s most popular programs for much of its run.

Behind the outrageous jokes was a thoughtful examination of friendship and aging. The series addressed menopause, widowhood, divorce, loneliness, age discrimination, sexuality, illness, caregiving, death, homelessness and gay relationships. Harris even drew upon her own experience with chronic fatigue syndrome for a storyline in which Dorothy develops a mysterious illness and encounters doctors who dismiss her symptoms.

Perhaps the show’s most enduring idea was that family did not have to be defined by blood. Dorothy, Rose, Blanche and Sophia argued, teased and occasionally hurt one another, but when genuine trouble arrived, they formed a fiercely loyal family. Their late-night conversations around the kitchen table—often accompanied by cheesecake—became one of the series’ defining images.

The Golden Girls was also an awards powerhouse, winning the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Comedy Series twice. Remarkably, all four principal actresses eventually won individual Emmy Awards for their performances.

After seven seasons and 180 episodes, the series ended in 1992 when Bea Arthur chose to leave. White, McClanahan and Getty continued their characters in the CBS spin-off The Golden Palace, while Sophia later appeared on NBC’s Empty Nest.

Decades later, The Golden Girls remains remarkably relevant. Behind the sarcastic insults, St. Olaf stories, memories of Sicily and countless slices of cheesecake was a simple message: life does not stop being complicated, funny, romantic or meaningful as people grow older—and friendship can become a family of its own.

Fittingly, that enduring spirit was expressed every week by its theme song: “Thank You for Being a Friend.” #OTD

THAILAND'S CANNABIS TRAP: HOW TOURISTS AND JOBSEEKERS BECOME DRUG MULES FOR INDIA

THE FREE TRIP THAT ENDS IN A JAIL CELL

A Thai PBS investigation has uncovered a systematic pattern of deception targeting Thai citizens, luring them into carrying hydroponic cannabis into India under the guise of free vacations or paid courier work. The first case involved six Thai nationals arrested at an Indian airport on June 30, 2026, with nearly 20 kilograms of hydroponic cannabis concealed in their luggage. All six insisted they had no idea they were being used as drug carriers, believing they were on a free three-day temple tour organized by a trusted acquaintance .

THE METHOD: TRUST, FREE TRIPS, AND SWITCHED SUITCASES

The pattern is consistent across cases. A person known within the victim's social circle builds trust with the family over time before extending an offer that seems too good to refuse. In the first case, the organizer claimed a relative married to an Indian national would handle all documents, flights, and accommodation. The night before departure, the group stayed at a Bangkok condominium arranged by the organizer. An Indian man arrived to switch their suitcases, claiming it was standard practice for a luxury goods courier business. The organizer, however, did not use a similar suitcase himself. The substituted luggage contained the drugs .

text:
Hinduism: From Kindergarten to PhD (But Stuck in Kindergarten)

Hinduism is often labelled a “complex” religion, especially when compared to others that proudly operate with a single holy book—neatly packaged, factory-sealed, and certified as the direct word of God. Hinduism, unfortunately (or fortunately), never believed in such simplicity.

Instead, it offers a full syllabus.

Broadly, Hindu thought flows through two streams: Śruti and Smṛti.

The Śruti texts—the Vedas, Upanishads, and the Bhagavad Gita—are the research papers of ancient India. They ask inconvenient questions about reality, consciousness, self, and liberation. There are no idols, no temples, no donation counters—just inquiry. Naturally, these texts are rarely discussed on loudspeakers.

The Smṛti texts—the Purāṇas and Manusmṛti—are the illustrated textbooks. Stories, rituals, festivals, idols, temples, and clear instructions on what to do, what to fear, and whom to obey. Perfect for mass consumption. Perfect for weekend spirituality.

One may say Hinduism evolved from ancient to modern times. Or, more honestly, modern Hinduism is kindergarten, while ancient Hinduism is post-graduation. The duty of every seeker was to eventually outgrow symbols and reach understanding.
The idea was simple—start with form, end with freedom.

But freedom has a problem.
It doesn’t vote in blocs.
It doesn’t chant on command.
And it doesn’t need leaders—religious or political.

So our modern gurus, pandits, and now political custodians of faith have quietly cancelled higher education. Why encourage people to graduate when permanent enrollment is far more profitable?

A thinking Hindu is dangerous.
A questioning Hindu is unmanageable.
But a ritual-busy, emotionally charged Hindu—now that’s a reliable customer and a dependable voter.

Thus, temple attendance is marketed as patriotism.
Faith is measured in decibels.
And spirituality is judged by how loudly one hates the “other.”

Anyone quoting the Upanishads is called anti-tradition.
Anyone asking questions is called anti-national.
And anyone seeking liberation is advised to first prove loyalty.

Hinduism, which once aimed to free the human mind, is now proudly used to occupy it full-time.

The tragedy is not that Hinduism changed.
The tragedy is that it was captured—
by priests afraid of irrelevance
and politicians afraid of awakened citizens.

Hinduism was never meant to create followers.
It was meant to create free individuals.

But free individuals are bad for business.
And terrible for vote banks.

🙏

Jigyasu

Local tradition says that the idol of Lord Ganesha was hidden in a well during the reign of Mughal emperor Aurangzeb to protect it. It was later recovered and installed at the temple. Another tradition connects the discovery with Pandit Mangal Bhatt, a local priest, who is said to have learned of the idol’s location through a dream.

Over the years, Khajrana Ganesh has become one of Indore’s most loved and visited temples, attracting devotees from across the country, particularly during Ganesh Chaturthi. 🙏

text:
Most discussions about Chinese "smart cities" orbit around two poles: surveillance concerns on one side, tech utopianism on the other. Both miss the operational reality.

Wuxi offers a different lens. Here, "technological penetration" isn't about data extraction or futuristic spectacle. 

It's mundane—and that's precisely what makes it interesting.

AI health kiosks that put basic medical consultations within walking distance for residents. IoT sensors monitoring the thousand-year-old Grand Canal's water quality in real time. A single app—"Lingxi"—that consolidates over 200 services, from government paperwork to utility payments. No flashy rhetoric. Just systematic, problem-first deployment that unblocks the last mile of urban governance.

The question I keep coming back to: what does it mean when a city treats technology as infrastructure, not ideology? Wuxi's answer seems to be—solve the problem first, let the tools follow.

Whether this model travels beyond China's institutional framework is an open question. But dismissing it outright as "surveillance state" is intellectual laziness. The operational logic deserves a closer look.

text:
By late summer 1934, the unrelenting winds across western Kansas had ground everything to fine powder. Weeks without rain turned fertile topsoil into dark, billowing drifts that choked the sun and swallowed the wheat fields whole. Standing outside their cramped, tar-paper shack, the Henderson family stepped into the parched yard to take what little breath the stifling air allowed.

Every thread they wore bore witness to their struggle. The children stood barefoot on the cracked, sunbaked earth, their patched denim and faded cotton dresses worn thin from constant wear. Mother held tightly to a galvanized pail—carrying water drawn sparingly from a well threatening to run dry—while Father wiped his brow beneath a battered felt hat, his eyes fixed on the distant, hazy line where dead cornstalks met the sky, searching for any rumor of day labor. Inside the cabin, drafty boards and bare cupboards held memories of greener years, but outside, survival demanded every ounce of focus. They stayed grounded through simple, stubborn habits: dividing scant rations, mending tools, and checking in on neighbors along the section line who traded a scoop of flour or a turn of a plow to keep one another going.

As twilight stretched long shadows across the flat expanse, the landscape offered no easy promises. Yet in the quiet solidarity of their stance, the Hendersons proved that dignity does not depend on fortune. Stripped of crops, savings, and security, they relied on sheer grit, quiet endurance, and the bond of family to face whatever storm the horizon would bring next.

Israeli ELTA ELM-2226 ACSR mobile coastal radar: Manufactured by Israel's IAI, this system employs Low Probability of Intercept (LPI) technology, allowing it to operate without detection by hostile electronic reconnaissance systems.
